maintopic: STATEMENT ON DELIVERY QUOTA POSITION IN WESTERN CANADA
STATEMENT ON DELIVERY QUOTA POSITION IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform hon. members of the grain delivery quota position
in western Canada. As at June 27 there were 62 stations on a 4 bushel quota, 607 on a 5 bushel quota and 1,325 on a 6 bushel quota. The railways have been instructed to give priority to those stations on a low quota, and those producers on 4 and 5 bushel quotas can be assured, therefore, that box cars will be available shortly.
Hon. members from western Canada in particular will wish to have some indication of the maximum quota levels which may be reached this crop year. I discussed this subject with officials of the Canadian wheat board yesterday and can now inform the house that an effort will be made to have all stations on a 7 bushel quota by the end of the crop year.
I wish to make it perfectly clear that no complete assurance can be given to producers at this time that it will be possible for them to deliver a full 7 bushel quota. There are several hundred stations presently on a 6 bushel quota where space is now available, and in order to take full advantage of the situation the board will issue instructions today that producers at these stations may deliver grain against a 7 bushel quota. As space becomes available at other stations the elevator agents will advise the Canadian wheat board when there is sufficient space to warrant an increase to a 7 bushel quota.
Under the extremely adverse conditions now prevailing in western Canada it is impossible to predict with any degree of accuracy the extent to which producers may wish to avail themselves of delivery opportunities. Many producers may in fact wish to retain supplies of grain on their farms for feed and seed purposes. In other areas where crop conditions are more favourable producers 90205-6-4531
may wish to deliver their grain to the maximum extent possible. It is for this particular reason that, whereas producers are assured of a full 6 bushel quota, the extent to which deliveries may be made against the 7 bushel quota may vary as between stations and areas.
With my full approval the Canadian wheat board will endeavour to equalize delivery opportunity to the extent possible, consistent with the No. 1 task of ensuring that supplies of grains and grades of grain are available to meet export and domestic commitments.

subtopic: DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-ANNOUNCEMENT OF FEDERAL AID
DROUGHT CONDITIONS IN WEST-ANNOUNCEMENT OF FEDERAL AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Prime Minister informed the house of the grave drought conditions prevailing in western Canada and outlined certain actions to be implemented by the government to assist farmers in obtaining adequate supplies of fodder.
In addition to fodder requirements the government and the Canadian wheat board have received requests from certain areas for the retention of stocks of wheat, oats and barley in store, country elevators, to fulfil anticipated local requirements. Following discussions with officials of the wheat board I am pleased to inform the house that the board is now prepared to facilitate the holding of necessary grain supplies for local sale purposes provided prior arrangements are completed with the local authorities with respect to the payment of carrying charges on stocks held for this purpose.
Accordingly the Canadian wheat board will issue instructions today authorizing local elevator companies, when approached by municipal authorities requesting stocks of specific grain to be held for local side, to immediately contact the board. The board will then enter into provisional sales contracts with the company on the understanding that carrying charges are for the account of the municipality. In the event that more stocks are contracted for than are ultimately required, the board will agree to cancel the provisional sales contract and the balance of the stocks will be reclaimed by the board, which will again assume the carrying charges.
I have had discussions with the provincial ministers of agriculture of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and I am today trying to contact

the minister of agriculture of Alberta, to let them know of this action immediately. I do not think I need tell the house that this action is now being taken to avoid a recurrence of what happened in 1937 and 1938 in the prairies.

The representatives of the churches concerned were informed that Canada supported the resolution of April 22 of the general assembly which set up a subcommittee to inquire into the situation in Angola because the government considered that the resolution offered a moderate and helpful approach to a complicated subject, and the Canadian government hoped that the subcommittee would be able to make recommendations

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 27, consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Benidickson.
(Translation):

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was dealing with the rather unpleasant records to whidh four years of Conservative administration in this country had led. Yet, in view of those records I mentioned last night, the Conservatives persist in saying that the situation in Canada could not be better. As

I cannot believe that the government is either blind or in bad faith, let me say this-the Conservative party has beaten another record, that of naivety.
In the light of all those rather unenviable records and their disastrous results for the nation, it is not surprising to find that the Conservative members are reluctant to participate in this debate. When you see them so silent, you would think they are attending someone in the throes of death. There is not even a whisper. They are awaiting the demise of this government and trying to keep it alive a little longer by giving it shots in the arm like the Coyne affair, which I am sure, will have no effect whatsoever.
After months of anguish and hesitation on the part of the Minister of Finance and of anxious expectation on the part of our people, the Minister of Finance, in all his greatness, has at long last condescended, at the very last moment, to submit a financial report on the country's business together with the budget for this fiscal year which is a few months old already.
Considering how long it had taken to prepare it, we were entitled to expect, if not a masterpiece, at least a decent piece of work, but the minister just gave us a daub, and a bad one at that.
As Mr. Paul Sauriol wrote in Le Devoir of June 22, 1961:
That document scarcely answered the public's expectation. It contained no surprise and hardly any changes in the taxpayer's yearly return- Such a budget should make one think, because it reflects disquieting problems in our national economy.
The minister had indicated an expansionist fiscal policy, but as I said last night at the beginning of my remarks, the expansionist trend of the budget only applies to the deficit.
There are, of course, new tariff barriers in it and on the whole it will add to the burden for the Canadian taxpayer.
The average Canadian will suffer from the devaluation of the Canadian dollar more than he will benefit.
Anyhow, that fluctuation is a new contradiction, or rather a new about-face in fiscal matters on the part of the minister.
In his budget speech, last year, the minister had objected to all suggestions in favour of a fluctuating Canadian dollar on the world market, and vehemently denounced it, stating that such a policy would necessarily require the purchase of uncalculable amounts of American dollars, which would be a bad thing for our economy.
Yet, this year, he advocates the policy which Ihe had radically rejected at that time.
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau
What will be the direct results of this policy for the Canadians? We will have to pay more for imported goods and heaven knows how much we must rely on imports for our day to day requirements.
This is what was written by Mr. Norman Campbell, parliamentary reporter for the Ottawa Citizen in the June 21 issue of that paper:
There is nothing much in the budget for the consumers except the prospect of higher prices.
This is where we stand after four years of a Conservative administration. From its prosperous position of 1957, Canada has now fallen to the depths of an economic slump. We are facing all kinds of economic difficulties resulting in unemployment and concern for thousands of families who only ask to be allowed to work, to live and to share in the tremendous resources with which this country was endowed by Providence.
We are all the more entitled to demand from the Conservative government an account of the administration of the nation's business entrusted to them by the people, since the present government had promised them the moon and stars.
Everybody remembers the famous statement made by the Conservative leader:
As long as I am Prime Minister of Canada, no one will suffer.
In another sermon delivered before the young Conservatives of eastern Quebec, in Quebec city, on December 8, 1957, he made the following statement as reported in La Presse for December 9:
The Conservative party considers it its mission to rebuild the country from its ruins... You can be sure that it will not fail in its task and that, in its activities, it will never forget the beauty and greatness of our dear country.
Mr. Speaker, I am willing to believe the Prime Minister when he claims that he has the beauty and greatness of our dear country at heart, but I readily maintain that the result of his four years of administration has proved that he and the members of his government do not have the required administrative qualifications to achieve that purpose.
They took over a prosperous Canada and are leading it to bankruptcy. If the government has its reasons to demand the resignation of the governor of the Bank of Canada, if it passes a special act to remove him, the Canadian people are justified in withdrawing their confidence from the present government and they are logical in doing so. They will be justified in replacing this government by another at the next rendering of accounts when we go to the country.
Yes, members on the government side should indeed be hesitant to participate in the present debate.

The Budget-Mr. Rouleau
In order to distract the public's attention from the sad state of the nation's affairs, the Conservative government has been making, through its Minister of Finance, a lot of fuss about the Coyne incident, and this just before the budget presentation.
If that incident were not so tragic, it could be called: A comedy in* three acts by Donald Fleming. Producer: Donald Fleming; Star actor: Donald Fleming; Publicity: Donald Fleming.
In the first act enters the Minister of Finance cast in the part of an offended virgin; he goes into a tirade-the governor of the Bank of Canada had a $25,000 a year pension voted for himself, without my knowledge. What a shame. He must resign, he has to go at once.
But the strange and bewildering thing is that this pension was voted 16 months ago by the board of directors appointed by the Minister of Finance himself, and in the presence of the assistant deputy minister of finance. Surely all these people must keep quite a lot of secrets from the Minister of Finance, since, during a period of 16 months, he was kept unaware of what had been going on in an organization of which he is the boss on behalf of the Canadian taxpayers.
Then the curtain rises on act two. The scene has changed. Enters the same actor in a new part and with new lines.
The governor's pension hovers in the background. Now, the governor must quit because he and the government do not agree on economic and monetary policies.
All this is quite hard to follow. The plot of the play is getting complicated. In 1954, the present Minister of Finance who then sat on the banking and commerce committee agreed* with Mr. Graham Towers, who was then governor of the Bank of Canada, that in case of a serious difference between the governor and the government in matters of economic and monetary policy the governor was bound to resign.
Since he took over as Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Eglinton went through a certain evolution and has been contending for the last four years, especially when faced with criticism concerning credit limitations, that he could not do a thing because monetary policy was outside his realm and within the exclusive province of the Bank of Canada.
And yet in February 1961, he asserted in the house that there was no dispute between him and the governor of the Bank of Canada. So, according to the minister, they were on good terms then. In February 1961, there was the brotherly hug and the curtain fell on the second act.


Then the curtain rises again on the third and final act, to wind up the play.
It was the budget speech. The minister gave a good performance. His lines kept him going during two and three quarters hours, and the minister did not even stop for a drink. During those 165 minutes of speech, he barely spoke a few minutes in French for the gallery.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was more than previously.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That torrent of words did not give rise to a strong reaction. To hide the omissions, the deficiencies of his speech, the minister wound up in a high voice, he looked up, pointed an angry finger and ruthlessly condemned the governor of the Bank of Canada: "There is the man responsible for all our ills. It is because of him that we have deficits and unemployment, his policy is wrong, he must go, he must resign. If he does not resign, I shall throw him out." Exit the governor. The minister calmly resumes his seat and the curtain falls. The volunteer firemen gratefully enter to put out the fire.
The audience-in this case the Canadian taxpayer-remains puzzled and again it has to pay the cost.
Deficits will continue to accumulate; the debt will continue to rise; the servicing of the debt will continue to increase; consumer products will be more expensive; unemployment, unfortunately, will still exist, and next year, before the election, someone will be found to bear the blame for the government's deficiencies.
For the characteristic of this government is to find someone on whom to cast the blame. There must be a scapegoat to explain the bad administration of the nation's business, resulting from inexperience, incompetence, lack of any sense of responsibility, indecision and complacency.
We could forgive all that to the present regime when it took over four years ago. The government was then progressing timidly, like a child taking its first steps. But today, the government, without ever having reached adulthood, is proceeding with the clumsy gait of a centenarian. The government is already suffering from senility.
Four years ago, our friends opposite made their first faltering steps, tripping on the minutest speck of dust, accusing their Liberal predecessors of being the cause of their failure or throwing themselves into the latter's bosom saying: "Tell us what to do, save us please."

Today in the throes of death, they are looking for scapegoats and behaving like old people who, having made a mess of their own lives, are in despair and blame both God and men for their failure. But they are the only ones to blame.
Still, they received a nice inheritance. The finances of the country were in order, prosperity was the attribute of Canada which caused the nations of the world to wonder in awe.
If, during those four years, the opposition have been critical-as it had good cause to be-they have also expressed their views and put forward concrete suggestions. Those suggestions fell upon deaf ears.
And now the governor of the Bank of Canada is being blamed for the whole thing. Long before today we have had occasion to say how much we disagreed with his policy. The minister used to reply that he was in agreement with the governor. We had no call to demand his resignation. We feel that when a public servant, whoever he might be, is called upon to advise the government, he has a strict duty to carry out its orders, or else he ought to tender his resignation. If he fails to do this, the government must immediately take action.
According to the minister in February 1961, only four months ago, there was no disagreement between him and the governor. Suddenly, just before the budget is brought in, the conflict breaks out.
Under those circumstances the opposition and the people of Canada have a right to ask that light be shed on the matter, that the governor and the minister be summoned before the banking and commerce committee to explain their positions so that facts may be assessed on their merits.
To our fair request the minister's answer is no. He will have only himself to blame if we harbour doubts and if the people of Canada are not satisfied.
Because of the conflict between the two men, the budget was introduced without the assistance of the governor of the Bank of Canada. He was not consulted nor even advised. This is a further source of concern to Canadian taxpayers, businessmen, industrial leaders, financial institutions and nations that do business with Canada. In the last few years, the Conservative government should have been fighting unemployment. Instead of this they have been fighting inflation through credit restrictions. Today we are faced with the results of that mistake.
The last budget is leading the ship of the nation into uncharted seas.
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
The experience of the last four years prevents us from trusting the pilot, in this case the Minister of Finance.
Our only hope now is to change the pilot before the ship goes down.
Directors who commit error upon error and accumulate deficits would not be kept long at the head of any corporation. The same thing applies to the government. This country's shareholders do not want to face bankruptcy; they look forward to the day when they can change their board of directors, before it is too late.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget is always a subject of major interest in any session. This year a desperate government, well aware of the political erosion it has suffered in the last two sessions as a result of its haughty contempt for parliament and its unbridled lust for power, has staked all its chances on the budget. It is the kind of budget that might be expected under those circumstances.
It is a budget full of pretence. It claims to be anti-inflationary. It is nothing of the kind. It is a delusive budget. It seeks to make people think they will be taxed less when the fact is that they will be required to pay more in taxes. It seeks to make people think that the government is holding the line against inflation when it is not.
It is a cynical budget. It contradicts what the government has been saying and doing. It is an opiate budget. The government openly boasts that the public has a short memory and can be made to forget the past as well as the present welter of the government's own contradictions.

The Budget-Mr. Chewier
It is a transparent budget. Its pose cannot hide its timing and purpose. It is an illusory-budget. It proposes changes, large in number but small in individual extent in every case, and seeks to create the impression of importance by their mere multiplicity. The banquet table is long. It is well dressed. The best silver and china are used. The lackeys are well trained, but the fare is thin. The guests have left unsatisfied.

speechtext: What is the quotation from?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those are not my words. They are the words of the Minister of Finance when in the opposition he spoke in this house during the consideration of the budget on March 21, 1957. They were words which he addressed to the house four years ago concerning the last balanced budget which this country has seen.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I now wish to turn to another matter and address myself particularly to the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion), because he did take part in the budget discussion.
In fact, he spent minutes congratulating the Minister of Finance for his masterful speech.
It is usual for an hon. member to congratulate the Minister of Finance, but when a member of the same cabinet commends his colleague, it is something rather strange, because in fact, he congratulates himself.
Does that not show a lack of solidarity as between members of the same cabinet? We had occasion in the past to witness a deep seated difference of opinion between the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) and some of his colleagues. I refer to the case of the C.B.C. producers' strike in Montreal. The Minister of Transport said the strike was legal, while the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) called it illegal. Placed between the two was the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), who did not dare to say whether it was legal or not.
The Secretary of State spoke of last year's budget. It matters little, he said, if the December forecasts met with adverse winds.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, last year's budget met with highly adverse winds.
In analysing this budget, there are four different aspects to consider.
First, let us look at the forecasting errors of the Minister of Finance. Last year, he predicted that we would have a surplus of $12 million. What happened? He first said there would be a deficit of $285 million, and it finally reached $345 million.

Surely, that is a very serious error, which had never been committed before by a Minister of Finance in bringing down his budget.
Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that in the circumstances the estimated deficit of $650 million for the current year will prove more accurate?
Last year the Minister of Finance told us that unemployment would disappear with the melting of the snow. Yet we have now a greater number of unemployed than we ever had in the past 20 years.
The Conservatives claim that this is something they inherited from the Liberals.
The truth is, they cannot stand on their own feet, they cannot accept their own responsibilities.
They always have to find an excuse, the Coyne case for instance.
The Minister of Labour stated in early March, 1960 that the 1958 recession was over.
That statement was true. How, then, can the Conservatives claim that the Liberals are responsible for the new recession which began only in 1960?
Last year we were told that the recession was over, that there would be prosperity throughout the country. Unemployment is on the rise. It has now reached 7 per cent of the labour force in Canada. Who should be blamed for that situation?
In 1957, the Liberals left the Conservatives a legacy worth recalling.
The Liberals left an unemployment insurance fund of $900 million. That fund has dropped to less than $100 million and yet the government does not make the slightest move to improve the situation.
The minister stated that the national product was going to increase by 6 per cent, but the increase was only 3 per cent.
Are we, in the circumstances, to put faith in the minister's budget forecast, when he says that the deficit will reach between $600 and $700 million?
Is it not more likely that the deficit will reach the billion dollar mark?
Another point: the omissions in the budget. The minister did not provide anything for farmers.
What cure did the Minister of Finance propose to the Canadian farmers? Not long ago, he made a speech in which he told farmers to work and to save money.
How could Canadian farmers, especially those from the province of Quebec, work and save money when they barely earned enough to make a decent living?

The dominion bureau of statistics has supplied figures to show it. In 1959, farmers net income was down 11 per cent; during the session, the Minister of Agriculture forecast that farm income in 1960 would be still lower than in 1959.
What is happening today, in 1961? At a time when farm income is steadily decreasing, the Conservative government advises the farmers that they must save and work; it provides nothing at all for them in the budget.
There is nothing either in the budget for underdeveloped areas. The budget provides nothing for our trade policy except for the maintenance of protectionism.
With one hand, the Minister of Finance promotes freer trade and with the other hand he leans towards protectionism.
Third, he said that interest rates would go down. If he actually has to borrow $1 billion, how will he manage to reduce interest rates? Moreover, he will have to get funds for the C.N.R., for all the crown corporations and for a number of non-budgetary items which I cannot enumerate because I have not enough time at my disposal.
That is, therefore, contradictory. If, on the one hand, interest rates are to go down, while the interest on the debt keeps on increasing, on the other, how will he succeed in borrowing those huge sums of money and reduce interest rates at the same time? Unless, of course, the person who is appointed as governor of the Bank of Canada increases the money supply, becomes the government's handyman and does exactly what the government tells him to do. If, by any chance, that happened, we would have inflation. Prices would go up, the cost of living would go up and, consequently, pensions would lose a great deal of their value.
Fourth, I should like to speak of the exchange rate. The devaluation of the Canadian dollar has been mentioned. The minister advocated a significant reduction in the value of the Canadian dollar. But when asked, in the house as well as during a press conference, what would be that significant devaluation, he refused to answer. However, his present stand is in direct contradiction with the one he adopted last year. Here is what he said about devaluating our dollar in his budget speech of March 31, 1960:
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier
An attempt by the government artificially to lower the external price of the Canadian dollar would involve borrowing or raising by taxes very large sums of money with which to buy up foreign exchange.
In other words, we would have embarked upon a gigantic financial speculation without any chance of success. Yet, this year he is embarking himself upon that gigantic speculative action he condemned last year.
Mr. Speaker, this gigantic speculation is the only action spelled out in the present budget. As the minister said, to significantly reduce the value of the Canadian dollar, we must buy American dollars. For how much? We do not know. How? We do not know either. Apart from the billion already referred to I do not think this is the right way to go about it. It is better to let the Canadian dollar finds its own level than to resort to artificial means of devaluating it.
The directors of the international monetary fund have already reminded the Canadian government of engagements entered into with that institution and, more particularly, of its pledge to maintain our currency at par. This will therefore entail heavy buying of American dollars. To reduce the value of the dollar is, consequently, to increase the cost of living, the cost of everything we import into this country. And everyone knows that we import much more than we export. This means, therefore, an increase in the cost of living. Recently, a probable one cent increase in the price of bread has been forecast.
The minister also favours an expansionist budget. It is obvious that this expansion will directly lead us toward inflation. The capital of the industrial development bank is to be increased from $160 to $400 million. But while the government propose to increase the capital of that bank, what steps are they proposing with respect of the economically underdeveloped areas? Not only is there not a single word in this budget about the underdeveloped areas of Canada, but no assistance is provided for them. No municipal fund where the municipalities could borrow. The municipalities will find it difficult to borrow in Canada. For a few years they have been borrowing in the United States at rates lower than in Canada; today, due to the devaluation of our dollar and the premium on the American dollar, they will not be able to borrow in the U.S. any more.
The real cause of the present economic stagnation is the fiscal and monetary policies of the government. They have increased long term expenditures instead of reducing taxes. They dealt with the recession as if it

The Budget-Mr. Chevrier were a depression. Long term expenditures have brought about budgetary deficits; we have now reached the fifth budget and the accumulated deficit reaches $2 billion. The government had to sell bonds to make up the deficit. The Bank of Canada had to increase the money supply by $1,700 million, or 16 per cent. The result was inflation, and the bank had to check the inflation.
The government had to borrow to make up its deficit, and in doing so, found itself in competition with private enterprise, corporations, companies, municipalities and provinces all across Canada. What did this mean? It had to raise interest rates, to the serious detriment of the small borrower, to the man in the street.
Interest on the debt went up by $300 million. The public bodies borrowed in the United States, as I said a moment ago.
The tightening of credit had disastrous effects on small borrowers, on trades people and merchants.
As for secondary industry, it suffered more than anyone else. All we have to do is to compare the present situation with conditions prevailing from 1945 to 1957 to know where things stand. Indeed, the London Economist, in an editorial dealing with the way in which Canada managed its business and budgeting, said this:
No country in the world has managed its economy as efficiently as Canada has done.
Yesterday, the Secretary of State spoke about textiles. He upbraided the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger) for what the latter had said with regard to that industry. Yet, no member in this house is as keen and shows greater interest in this matter which affects the people in his riding, as the hon. member. On several occasions, he rose in this house to defend their interests. He is interested in textile workers and has shown it on many occasions.
With regard to the textile industry in Canada I shall say that, in the last four years, several plants had to close down. I have a list here and can name them. To quote a single instance, in Hamilton, the very riding of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough), that industry was employing 1,000 workers. There are also textile plants at Grand'Mere, at Cornwall, three of which at least closed down-but never mind.
In the last four years, as was said in committee of the other place, the number of textile workers has decreased by 25,000. However, the crux of the matter is that the present government, whose members are facing me, had promised to settle that problem. The Prime Minister himself, when he travelled

through all ridings with textile mills, stated that, as soon as he took over he would protect that industry, thanks to his good management and adequate methods.
I lack the time to read those statements into the record, but as everybody knows, the Prime Minister of Canada declared that, once in power he would protect the textile industry as well as he had protected agriculture.
In 1958, he submitted to the house a bill known as the anti-dumping legislation in order to help the textile industry. Here is what a parliamentary correspondent, Mr. Richard Gwyn, had to say on June 1, 1959, under the heading:
(Text):
Government has means to curb textile imports
The government now has in its hands an instrument which could save the textile industry without any further action. This is Bill C-51, known as the "anti-dumping legislation."
C-51 gives revenue minister George Nowlan power to slap high tariffs on any goods dumped on the Canadian market at prices lower than production costs plus a fair profit mark-up.
More important he has the power to place prohibitive tariffs on goods coming in from countries where production costs are far below those of Canada.-
Only trouble is the government hasn't used C-51, though it has been on the statute books a year.
(Translation):
That legislation was passed by parliament almost three years ago. Why is it not used?
(Text):

The point is that the Minister of Finance said at the time that this was going to be of tremendous assistance to the textile industry, but why has the government not used it? I doubt very much if it has used it on more than half a dozen occasions.

The Secretary of State referred to what the Bennett government had done with regard to textile mills. Let me say to him that from 1930 to 1935, when the Bennett government was in office, textile workers suffered as they suffer today, and notwithstanding the assertions of the minister, it does not seem that the problem can be settled through increased tariff protection. And to prove my point, I shall quote from a statement made by the president of the primary textile institute, Mr. Berry, before a Senate committee:
(Text):
Our position on the tariff could be put quite briefly, and it is this: We have just barely completed a three-years' review by the tariff board of tariffs on textiles, and whatever we might think

of the results, we must conclude that the revisions that have been made have been made within the framework of the present Canadian policy. We only have two comments to make on that policy, and one is that a policy which allows penetration into a market to the extent which has become apparent in our business is not likely to be a good policy for Canada for an indefinite period. Our views on that are somewhat supported, we think, by an observation that the tariff board itself made, in their first report in the textile series, having this to say: "There may be recommended for the industry a measure of assistance that will permit it to continue to fight for its existence at least until such time as there may be initiated by the proper authority a carefully considered decision on high policy regarding the future of the industry." This indicates to us that the board was probably then in need of policy direction, and in so far as we are aware none followed.
That was the statement.
(Translation):
Mr. Berry made that statement in reply to a question. When someone asked whether he anticipated any tariff assistance, he said no, just as he had said in the Senate committee, as reported on page 1014 of the record of proceedings.

The hon. member for Stormont seems to be very jealous of his prerogatives as a member of parliament, and that no one should interfere in his constituency. Well, Mr. Speaker, do you think even if you are invited by the constituents of the hon. member you should not interfere? I have been invited on numerous occasions. I should like to say to this house that I receive perhaps as much mail from the constituency of Stormont as does the hon. member himself. I cannot explain why the hon. member's constituents come to me for advice. They do, they have and they will continue to do so. It is easy for me to understand why the hon. member is annoyed. He is annoyed not so much at me-

speechtext: Just bragging again.

He is annoyed at himself because his constituents will not come to him. The proof of this lies in the fact that on matters concerning the St. Lawrence seaway, particularly those having to do with
The Budget-Mr. Chevrier pilotage, they came to me. Is it not strange that they came to the member for Laurier and not to the member for Stormont? A debate took place on that legislation for almost two days. The member for Stormont was not even in his seat. The bill was referred to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. We had a discussion that lasted two days. Again the member for Stormont was not in his seat except in the dying hours, and then only at the request of the hon. member for Port Arthur who said, "Where is the member for Stormont?" He came in and this is what he said:
I am vitally concerned with anything having to do with the seaway but I am not directly concerned with the pilots as there are none of them residents in my area.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are several sitting right behind you now.
The hon. member did not even know there were pilots in his riding. There have been pilots in the constituency of Stormont since time immemorial; since I was a child I remember seeing pilots walking up and down the streets. Furthermore, the Minister of Transport was asked whether there were any pilots in Cornwall and he said "Yes, sure, there is a pool of pilots that has been established there; there are 21 or 24."
Here is this man who makes a vicious attack on me, and I understand why. Again I say it is not because of me. He is annoyed at himself, and he is doing his constituents a great disservice first when he says there are no pilots in his riding. I am sure they would like that. Second, he is also doing his constituents a great disservice when he says that the constituency of Stormont, particularly Cornwall, is a depressed area. Imagine a member of parliament rising in the house and so maligning his constituency by saying that it is a depressed area.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the member for Niagara Falls?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

What do you think industry is going to do in that respect? Then again he complained bitterly about the locks being on the United States side, and the place being stranded, and so forth. He seems to forget entirely that there is a 27-foot waterway right in front of Cornwall on the Canadian side from St. Regis island right up to the dike. It is so patent that the Minister of Public Works would not be spending $400,000 and perhaps more to put a wharf there if there was not a deep-sea channel in order to bring deep-sea vessels. Therefore when he suggests there are no 27-foot facilities again he is maligning his constituency and doing his constituents great harm. He is not only

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

At the end of my remarks. He says the seaway building which has been erected there is not appreciated. Well, the seaway building employs almost 150 people. I see he has been not only firing some of those who were there before but he is employing, I am sure, friends of his in this building. There is no doubt that this building which he depreciates on the one hand is one in which he is most anxious to put workers on the other.
Again, he does not like the idea of a power block having been set aside for United States industrial development and no power block for the province of Ontario. He says that is the fault of the then member for Stormont and the former minister of transport, who should have seen to that. Well, we all know who is in charge of the government of the province of Ontario. Premier Frost is the head of that government. I am told he is a very close friend of the member for Stormont. They are great buddies; they see each other quite frequently. I hope the member for Stormont will make the required representations so that Cornwall and the whole St. Lawrence valley in that area will get a block of power for industrial development in the same manner and to the same extent as did the New York side of the line.
I say the member for Stormont has ignored the pilots who live in his riding. He calls his constituency a depressed area. He emphatically states no 27-foot facilities are established there. In saying these things he is doing great harm to the constituency. He says that the canal ends in a high wall 80 feet in length. But a turning basin has been made available there in the same way as there is a turning basin in the Lachine canal so that ships can move in and out. I say that no one is doing more harm to his constituency than is the hon. member by his statements.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), in a desperate effort, tried to have the house believe that the new budget did not have the support of the Canadian people.
You need only read the comments in the press, the statements made by businessmen in various segments of the economy, to realize that the Canadian people support this budget.
In fact, according to the Canadian Press, the primary textile institute has stated, following the tariff changes announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his budget speech, that some aspects of those changes are encouraging for the primary textile industry in Canada. The institute stressed the fact that the government's decision not to lower tariffs on textile products was particularly welcome in view of the competition from Asian countries.
Ever since he has been in this house, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) has been the champion of the textile industry in Canada and I wish to commend him for that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Without success.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In fact, the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin) even commended last year the hon. member for Sherbrooke for his courage and efforts in favour of the textile industry.
When this government took over, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals had completely sabotaged the textile industry. Everything had to be built up again. I have here a brief of the primary textile institute which praises the Minister of Finance because, in his budget,

he began to put the tiller right so that the textile industry may live again the life of yesteryears.
Besides, the Canadian exporters, according to Mr. John McDerby, general manager of the Canadian exporters association, find the Fleming budget satisfactory, generally speaking.
The Canadian automobile association, which has a membership of 600,000, commended the government for having granted its request for the abolition of the 74 per cent excise tax on passenger cars.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) did not mention that. He said that the Fleming budget did not meet the needs of Canadians.
However, I have here the many statements made by businessmen in this country.
In the cigarette manufacturing industry, for instance, Mr. J. H. Devlin, chairman of the Rothman company, said he was satisfied with the change announced in the excise tax on cigarettes. He said that the decrease in excise tax would result in longer cigarettes and an increase of tobacco purchases by the Canadian industry. Mr. Devlin added that tobacco purchases will increase by nearly 10 million pounds compared to last year.
Speaking for the farmers and the tobacco growers of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm riding, I should like to congratulate the minister for having taken this step which will prompt the tobacco growers to increase their production and thus to obtain higher returns.
Mr. John Magee, secretary of the Canadian trucking association, spoke very highly of the decision taken by the government in its new budget to increase the capital of the industrial development bank so that it will now be able to lend up to $400 million. Before, the credit margin was only of $160 million. Moreover, the new budget gives the bank the right to loan money to all groups of industries.
Mr. Speaker, I have only given the testimony of a few Canadian industrialists. The newspapers are filled with them, as one can see in reading the financial pages.
Only the Liberals are disappointed. They are not satisfied, because they realize that their popularity is now going down in the country. They know that they are disappearing from the electoral map and that they will probably disappear for good unless they amalgamate with the New party to have at least a few representatives in a corner of the house.
I have here a copy of Le Devoir of Tuesday, June 27, 1961, where I find this:
The Budget-Mr. Pigeon
Liberal party and N.P. amalgamation recommended by Liberals.
Milford Bay-To the dismay of the majority of the delegates who were at a dance party, a group of young Liberals of the Ontario association of young Liberals adopted a resolution recommending the amalgamation of the Liberal party with the New party in order to defeat the Progressive Conservatives.
The Liberals themselves admit they are defeated. They know that the voters have no more confidence in them, but, in order to stay in the opposition after the next election, they want to amalgamate with the New party, for they know that they will disappear from the electoral map, because they have lost contact with the people. Besides, they have always been remote from the people, they have never cared for the people.
Here is what I read, Mr. Speaker:
Wheat producers favoured by the budget.
The farmers form an important class. The Liberals speak of unemployment, but they forget the statement of their leader (Mr. Pearson). Time magazine of February 17, 1958 reported the following on page 14:
It would be stupid and unfair to blame the Conservatives for the present unemployment.
Therefore, the present Liberal leader criticizes the hon. member for Laurier, as well as all Liberal members in this house who claim that the Canadian government is responsible for unemployment. They are condemned by a statement of their own leader.
Then again, La Presse of September 23, 1960, reports a similar statement by Mr. Pearson:
Unemployment, he added, is the concern of all levels of government; it cannot be considered the sole responsibility of the federal government.
That is a further condemnation of the hon. member for Laurier and of the Liberals who sit in this house. That is why the young Ontario Liberals are right when they say their party should merge with the New party; they know that the political ground is getting slippery under their feet.
There is talk about unemployment. But here is what Mr. Georges Villeneuve, a former Liberal member of parliament for Roberval, had to say when the Liberals were in power, as reported on page 614 of Hansard for January 27, 1955:
Mr. Speaker, I find that in my constituency unemployment does not cause as much concern now as it did last year.
Not as much concern as last year. That means that in 1954, under a Liberal administration, unemployment was causing concern.
He added:
However we have seasonal unemployment and it is a problem which requires our attention as well as all our ingenuity if we want to solve it.

The Budget-Mr. Pigeon
That is a further condemnation by a Liberal member, Mr. Speaker.
I wish to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), and their colleagues in the cabinet for the efforts they are making to stimulate our economy.
Once more I encourage labour unions and industry to launch a campaign in order to have Canadians buy Canadian products.
Are we aware, for example, that each Canadian buys an average of foreign products amounting to $262 a year, when the corresponding average is only $48 in England and $28 in the United States?
I ask my fellow citizens to buy Canadian.
Canadian manufacturers of capital goods will now be in a better position to compete on foreign markets. To finance their sales abroad they will have the support of a company put up jointly by the larger banks of Canada and the federal government with a view to extending credit facilities to our exporters. It will be easier this way to find buyers for our products.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) is to be commended for such enterprising spirit.
Mr. T. R. McLagan, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association said in Montreal as reported in La Presse of October 28, 1960:
A strong policy promoting the sale of Canadian products remains one of the most realistic measures against unemployment.
He also added:
The lowering of production costs also seems to be a vital question, when we consider it in the light of exports. Canada is having difficulties getting into foreign markets, because her products are expensive and face very stiff competition. To answer that problem, we would have to sell cheaper, and we can do this only by materially reducing the production costs of our exported raw materials and finished products.
Of course, the cost of production is not the only barrier to the balance of our economy, but it does seem to be the main one, the most difficult one to overcome, because to do so, we must count on the co-operation of most of the people and of the leading labour and employer groups.
Mr. Speaker, there is much talk about unemployment. I have here a copy of the newspaper La Reforme, for November 19, 1960, which says:
Unemployment-a family problem and a provincial responsibility.
It is clearly stated in La Reforme that unemployment is a provincial and family responsibility.


Let the provincial government, which controls various sectors of the Quebec economy, highways, public works, construction of schools and hospitals, take its responsibilities.
Let it fulfil its promises, let it solve the unemployment problem.
Unemployment-a family problem and a provincial responsibility.
Let the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier reread the statement made by his leader, the Hon. Rene Hamel, minister of labour, on November 23, 1960:
The proportion of unemployed is going down in Quebec.
I also advise him to read an extract from the open letter published in La Presse of August 20, 1959, signed by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard), which read as follows:
The fight against unemployment is the concern of the government as well as of the governed, of management as well as of labour, of the public man as well as of the businessman, of industry as well as of banks. In a word, everyone must constructively co-operate in abolishing that social ill, while avoiding demagogy.
By the way, the hon. member for Laurier should carefully listen to this:
What must be avoided is any attempt to promote a political cause or ideal at the expense of those who are victims of a scourge like unemployment. There are too many demagogic politicians whose main ambition is to sell their product or to promote their own advancement by taking advantage of the least social disorder which, in their eyes, becomes only an accident, or a further opportunity in their prearranged pursuit of political aims.
These are formal statements; they are meant for the hon. members for Laurier, for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau), for St. Denis (Mr. Denis), and for St. Jean-Iberville-Na-pierville (Mr. Dupuis), and for all others of their ilk.
There are too many demagogic politicians whose main ambition is to sell their product or promote their own advancement.
The hon. member for Lapointe protests against the political ambitions of some of his colleagues.
Nevertheless, the hon. member for Laurier has no confidence in the future of this country, under a Conservative government.

I disapprove of the defeatism of those who think Canada would be destroyed and its whole population liquidated by the explosion of nuclear bombs.
The hon. member for Laurier, in opposing the Bomarc base, tried to deprive Quebec workers of hundreds of jobs. Curiously enough, however, he was at the same time confident in the future of Canada, in its development and prosperity, because he
The Budget-Mr. Howard accepted a directorship in the Provincial Bank of Canada in addition to the directorship he has held since last year in the North American Fund of Canada Ltd.
The Liberals are pessimistic, and the young Liberals are defeatists. They want to merge with the New party because they know they are doomed.
Their leader is not as brilliant as they and the hon. member for Laurier thought at one time.
The mayor of Portage la Prairie, Mr. Henderson, a candidate to the leadership of the Liberal party, made this statement in Winnipeg on January 7, 1956:
The Hon. Lester B. Pearson will be the choice of the convention, but he will not conquer the voters. He does not know the ordinary voter.
Mr. Speaker, I see here a sad thing and in concluding my remarks I wish to quote the following words of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent in the newspaper Le Devoir of September 4, 1958:
I miss active politics.
Mr. Speaker, do you know of any one member from the province of Quebec, including the new citizen of the province of Quebec, the ex-member for Stormont and present member for Laurier who took Mr. St. Laurent's defence when he was vulgarly excluded? No, they were all mute as a fish.
Mr. St. Laurent misses political activity. I think the young Liberals of this country are right when they think of joining the New party so that some of them at least might sit in the opposition.

719S	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Howard political machine to help them. I will say further that I am not too fussy about accepting the Liberal party and its adherents as such, as I see them in this house, into the New party; they are certainly Liberally minded people. But when it comes to accepting Union Nationale members, I say "never".
This is a somewhat strange budget debate, Mr. Speaker. We see how much reluctance there is on the part of Conservative members to associate themselves with the budget. They want to concern themselves more with engaging in smear tactics against a particular individual who has been in the news lately, and about whom I intend to say no more at this stage.
There was some thought that parliament might recess at the end of this week. It appears, though, that the suggestions or requests-perhaps one should call them demands -made by the Prime Minister earlier this week have pretty well eliminated that possibility. I am sure all hon. members at least from one point of view will not be too upset about that for it will afford them the opportunity to accept the warm and gracious invitation issued by Mr. Arthur Blakely of press gallery fame to attend a gathering this week end.
I was reading some debates of the house in earlier times-1954 was one-when some mention was made of reform of the other place. In that particular debate, in which the present Prime Minister took an active part together with Mr. Drew, the then leader of the Conservative party, reference was made to a period at least back to 1926-27 when Mr. Mackenzie King had made some efforts toward reformation of the other place, and how it was not too long ago that the present Prime Minister was campaigning on the basis of Senate reform.
I would say that this need for reform is no less urgent now than it was when the Prime Minister made those promises before 1957. In fact I think it is even more urgent in view of recent developments which have been taking place in the Senate. Perhaps I may indicate a case in point. I think the disdain and contempt with which Senator Roebuck treats other hon. members of the Senate divorce committee would indicate that some reformation is necessary. If that honourable senator seeks to develop his pet hobby to the point where he establishes himself in effect as a judge of divorce in the other place, that would indicate that we need even more movement in the direction of some reformation there, but not the type of reformation that the Prime Minister has engaged in, which was that followed by his predecessor, of merely


filling the Senate with people partial to his own points of view. However, Mr. Speaker, I intend to go no further into that matter. I saw that you were becoming a little active in your seat, and I took that as an indication that perhaps I had gone just about far enough along that line.
I should like to make reference, in so far as this budget is concerned, to a previous budget introduced by the Minister of Finance in 1959, and read just two short sentences from that budget speech as contained on page 2408 of Hansard of April 9 of that year. When dealing with one phase of economic matters in this country the Minister of Finance had this to say:
Advancing technology might have been expected to reduce the cost and selling price of many products to consumers. It is evident, however, that developments in corporation pricing policies, in labour organization and even in our political democracy are producing increased rigidities which inhibit the free play of competitive forces and thereby promote inflation and price increases.
Two years ago the Minister of .Finance, if we are to believe what he said in those statements-and there is some doubt that we should believe everything the minister says- had knowledge of the fact that, as he put it, there are increasing rigidities in the pricing policies of corporations which tend to depress what he called "the free play of competitive forces and thereby promote inflation and price increases".
I think it is commendable that the minister should have understood the force which is brought into play upon our economy by corporate price fixers and by what is perhaps loosely referred to as a system of administered prices, or in other words activities which are criminal in their operation and contrary to the statutes of this nation. Even more surprising, though, than the budget we have before us is the fact that the Minister of Finance two years ago recognized these factors and did nothing about them or was denied the opportunity to do anything about them by other members of the cabinet who would like to see other situations develop. However, I believe the Minister of Finance is a strong enough individual to get his point of view across on a number of occasions, and I am inclined to think that even though he recognized this two years ago, he really did not believe that his government wanted to do anything about it because it was contrary to the philosophy and intent of the Conservative party.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether at this stage I might call it one o'clock.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is a portent of things to come but I notice there is an equal number of Liberals and C.C.F. members in the house at the same time, or there was a moment ago.
There is a large contingent of members in the house who are advocates of what is known as the free enterprise system. I think it is unfortunate that the prescience of the Minister of Finance in 1959 in calling attention to the effects upon the economy of rigidity in price structures and price fixing was not carried forward in this particular budget, because the danger has not diminished during the passage of the last two years. In fact, it has increased as I shall show in a moment. There is a tendency on the part of the advocates of the so-called free enterprise system to equate free enterprise with lower prices, a better quality of goods and materials, more durable goods and the like. However, I think a much better case could be made for saying that the predominant relationship is of an altogether different kind. In other words, we can equate it with price fixing, with restrictions on production, with the carving up of markets for certain products and the like. Let me give hon. members a brief account of the record here in Canada during the past 11 years since 1950. This information was tabled in the house last year but I am afraid I do not have the reference to the specific sessional paper. It showed that the following industries and corporations in those industries have been found guilty of conspiracies and illegal actions under the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code. I find they include the glass industry, bread, baking, matches, rubberwear, tires, rubber footwear and all kinds of rubber goods; papers, both fine and coarse; electrical materials, wire and cable; farm fencing and other types of fencing; bedding, quilts, coal, roofing materials, pulpwood, culverts and transmission and conveyor belts. Companies in all these fields have been found guilty of illicit practices under the Combines Investigation Act and have been fined in the courts for engaging in price fixing.
It was not more than a couple of weeks ago in the United States, for instance, that attorney general Kennedy issued a statement to the effect that preliminary investigations there had indicated that in practically every major industrial field in the United States companies were engaged in the practice of fixing prices and increasing them by agreement without regard to the cost of production
The Budget-Mr. Howard of those commodities. Here in Canada I think this government has proven by the failure of the Minister of Finance to give concrete expression to those two sentences he mentioned in the 1959 budget that it is not really concerned with the welfare of consumers in this country, not really concerned with protecting them against encroachments upon their rights by corporate monopolies and oligopolies. This view is, I suggest, borne out also by this government's action in ramming a particularly obnoxious bill through the house amending the Combines Investigation Act in such a way as to make it easier for corporations to engage in these illicit practices and easier for them to escape detection. The sanctions and authorizations given, in effect, by last year's amendments to the Combines Investigation Act will illustrate this contention more clearly as time goes on.
On the general question of the operations undertaken under the Combines Investigation Act I should like to say it is extremely unfortunate that an investigation into the production and distribution and sale of raw fish in British Columbia has been postponed and delayed by a series of legal manoeuvres and skirmishes in the courts to prevent the restrictive trade practices commission from hearing the charges made by the director of investigation and research and coming to a determination with regard to them. That situation has existed because parliament has agreed to continue to extend the moratorium in respect to the activities of the fishing industry. That industry on the west coast is faced with continuation of a restrictive agreement regarding the number of boats which may engage in the herring production and fishing industry. I mention the herring fishery because of the restriction that exists in regard to it. The longer this continues the more difficult in an economic sense this will be for the fishing industry on the west coast.
We too often tend to think that competition brings benefits to the citizens of this nation through so-called free enterprise. We think of this free enterprise competition in relation to a number of different fields and often feel that it applies to different industries in a like manner. I suggest we have a number of different types of competition some of which may be beneficial but others which may be detrimental.
There exists competition in the field of prices to consumers and, I submit in this regard, there is very little which takes place in relation to major industries. There is perhaps a good deal more among smaller businesses because there does not exist there the same control in respect to competition and quality of goods.

The Budget-Mr. Howard
In terms of competition we can think of advertising in regard to the quality of the commodity which takes place in an attempt to make the products more attractive to the consumer. I submit that is all that is taking place in the way of competition. In Canada over the past number of years the original concept of competition which involved the price and quality of products has been misdirected and now relates almost exclusively to the field of advertising. I suggest that competition in the field of advertising does not in a general way result in benefits to consumers. We are all being inundated with advertisements appearing in newspapers, heard over the radio and seen on television, for example in regard to the various beneficial aspects of different types of toothpastes. I suggest that there is very little difference between the different brands except differences such as one being red, one being striped, one containing a special mint flavour and so on. Such toothpastes include a bit of glycerine, but in essence they are all the same. However, there is a great deal of competition regarding this particular product in the field of advertising which results not in any saving or increased quality to the consumer, but an increased cost. This same situation applies in respect to various other commodities. An individual may have a preference for a certain brand of cigarettes but, after all, cigarettes all contain tobacco and very likely have the same deleterious effect, if any.
An example of this type of so-called competition with lack of resultant benefits to the consumer was reflected by a report tabled in the house by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton). I might say that the tabling of this particular document was in direct contravention of an order of this house, but that did not seem to bother the minister at that time. That report indicated that so-called competition in industry had the direct result of increasing prices rather than decreasing them. I suggest when we find 25 per cent of the activity of the average drug company taking place in the field of advertising, which involves the inundation of doctors and others with gimmicks of all types, we also find this competition increases costs.
As I said earlier, smaller companies do not have the same control in regard to quality or price of products the larger corporations do, nor have they the control over the primary products involved. As an example of this suggestion, one might consider the local service station, which is a relatively small operation with no control over the primary product, because that control remains with


the oil companies. I suggest this same situation applies to all small industries and operators who are helpless against the large corporate structures. They are not being helped by this government at all in this regard.
In recent years there have been many comments heard in regard to a recession and a collapsing economy. In recent times this government has begun to think in terms in line with these comments and, after four years in office, it has decided to curtail this and that, in an attempt to correct the situation. I do not understand how this is going to help our economy, particularly in light of the extremely high degree of unemployment that has continually affected this country since this government took office. The Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny) suggested that this problem was a chronic one.
I suggest that in light of the unemployment picture and the economic position as it exists today we should consider how the corporate elements of this nation, which control our national resources, have fared during this period when so many people have attended bread lines and walked the streets day and night looking for work.
On page 32 of the Financial Post of May 13, 1961, there appeared an analysis of the economic conditions of a selected 313 companies, showing the changes which have taken place over the years, and particularly those changes which have taken place between 1959 and 1960; that period of time when the level of employment in this country was at its lowest. This is a statistical table of averages and accordingly individual companies may not fit into the picture presented here. However, we find the net value of the oil industry during this period of high unemployment, poverty and misery among the consumers increased by 3.8 per cent. We find the value of the metal industry increased by 6.8 per cent; the iron and steel industry by 2.8 per cent; the pulp and paper industry by 8.6 per cent; transportation by 1 per cent, merchandising by 8.2 per cent; the textile industry by 1.6 per cent-we heard a good deal about the difficulties of the textile industry today-the milling and grain industry by 4.1 per cent; construction by 3.4 per cent, and public utilities by 5.2 per cent. We also find that the food industry, representing a basic requirement of everyone in this country, increased in value by 15.5 per cent; the beverages industry by 6.1 per cent, miscellaneous by 4 per cent, and the lumbering industry by 4.1 per cent, with a total average increase in respect to 313 companies involving all our basic resources of 4.7 per cent.

All this took place at a time when, as I said, unemployment was rampant throughout the nation and when people were practically starving to death and getting rid of their furniture and other household goods and equipment which had been bought on a credit basis. In the face of this the Associate Minister of National Defence has the unmitigated gall to say that it is impolite to talk about unemployment; that it does not do a service to the country to talk about it. I can appreciate that he and his government, having the attachment that they have to certain vested interests in this nation, would not like to have unemployment discussed. They would like to see the working class continue to be subjected to this sort of illicit piracy which exists among corporations generally in this nation.
If the Minister of Finance two years ago had the foresight to say that the rigidities of the price system permitted inflation and higher prices and then did nothing about it, it is another indication why we have less and less reason to believe his statements and certainly not the forecasts and prognostications of the minister or of anybody else in the government of the day.
A number of phrases have been used and a number of words have been groped for to describe this particular budget. The Minister of Finance called it an economic budget, whatever that may mean. It is certainly a "deeper in debt" type of budget. One interesting development arising out of it I should like to mention is that a few years ago a bond conversion program was entered into by this government after a massive sales pitch by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, which had the direct effect of increasing interest rates. It was also supposed to regularize the debt picture of the country so that it would be easier to cope with it as the years went by. We are now in almost the same situation we were a couple of years ago out of which this bond conversion program was supposed to take us. In the 1961-62 fiscal year this government is going to have to find by borrowing one way or another $2,610 million. This amount is more than 40 per cent of the expenditures of this government for this particular year. This is an indication of what is happening with the government we have in office. Its sole concern is the paying off of election commitments made to those who financed the party to office. Coupled with the concern to continue in office is the intoxicated feeling that it received by virtue of the fact that it has power. That is its sole concern; in addition, stay in office regardless of the circumstances and how they affect anybody else, including the people of this country.
The Budget-Mr. Walker
The first impression I had with respect to classifying the budget by name when I listened to the Minister of Finance that glorious evening last week when he took so long to say so little was a word connected with his baby budget of last fall. I think we can properly classify this budget as a miscarriage.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have been trying to decide what all the sound and fury are about, Mr. Speaker, with respect to this budget. I have heard the opposition speakers and I have taken home their speeches to read at night, but I cannot find that any useful point has been raised in criticism of the budget of the Minister of Finance. If you will read it at home, Mr. Speaker, as I have read it-I know it was a long speech but it was a fascinating one; it cannot be digested all at one sitting-you will find that the answers are all there. It was a masterful exemplary presentation that we had the other night. For instance, everybody admits-the Leader of the Opposition and his party admitted it

that there should be an expansionist budget. The C.C.F. group admit that there should be an expansionist budget and there is. It is designed to increase the gross national product of Canada. This is the primary object of it and it comes at a time when it is very necessary to do that. It is designed to increase employment by hundreds of thousands and the minister has explained how this will come about. It is designed to lower interest rates, for which, of course, we need the co-operation of the Bank of Canada. Primarily, it is designed to lower the value of the Canadian dollar so that we can get our share of the export market.
Of necessity it is a deficit budget. Under these circumstances, when the government has these matters in mind, there is no other way of having a budget. The only other alternative is to increase taxes and to do so at this time would be to do harm to business by taking away capital which could be used in the plans of Canada for great expansion.
It is interesting to note that since this government came into power 80 per cent of all the tax-paying public, the people paying income tax, are paying less income tax than they did when we took over from the Liberals. May I also say that the Liberals advocated this. There is no criticism of us for having a deficit budget. There has been no criticism from the Leader of the Opposition. The other night in his press conference, when he was pressed by those able newspapermen who did not get anywhere with the Minister of Finance the night before, the Leader of the Opposition agreed that the government was right at this time to have a deficit budget.

The Budget-Mr. Walker Therefore, as far as policy and principle are concerned, we seem to be ad idem with the official opposition.
I make this statement. There would be no deficit even this year in our expansionist budget if we had not increased the social benefits to Canadians, the social justice payments, and if we had not increased the federal-provincial grants.
It is said that there will be a prospective deficit of $650 million. Well, the two items I have just mentioned make up $1 billion. When we took office the federal-provincial payments for 1956-57 were $689 million. In this current year they will amount to $1,470 million. When we took office old age pensions amounted to $379 million. In this current year they will be $607 million. In other words, in these two items alone there is a difference in excess of a billion dollars. If we had kept the even tenor of the Liberals' ways over the 22-year period and denied Canadians the social justice payments to which they were entitled and denied the provinces the payments to which they were entitled, instead of having a deficit of $650 million, we would be budgeting for a surplus of $350 million this year. Is there anybody who would want to take away hospital insurance which amounts to $274 million?
The other matter on which we have been criticized a great deal is the delay in the budget. Well I am not blaming any particular group or any particular member in the house but it is a fact that only recently were we able to get through the baby budget. We have in this session of parliament been delayed interminably. This is not a personal attack on anyone, but let us all examine ourselves and what we have done.
The longest session in the history of the House of Commons was in 1903, when the session lasted for 155 days. I believe that this is the 144th day of this session and the end is not in sight. May I just cite some examples? I had a statistician check some figures to ascertain certain things. Up to June 21 of this year the total number of pages of Hansard, Mr. Speaker, from November 18 to June 21 amounted to 6855. Let us take a member of parliament and ascertain what his contribution was. Let us take the last speaker, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). The estimated number of pages that the hon. member for Skeena filled in Hansard amounted to 125. The percentage of the hon. member's contribution to the total contribution of parliament in the way of words was 1.8 per cent, nearly 2 per cent. The number of days in the session up to June 21, my latest figure, was 138. The number of days consumed by the

hon. member for Skeena if he had started talking before the orders of the day when the house convened at 11 o'clock in the morning and continued through until 10.30 at night, would have been 2-J days.
The daily cost of operating the House of Commons, on the basis of an estimate appearing in Hansard of August 8, 1960, page 7757, is $20,000. The total cost, therefore, of having the benefit of the wisdom, advice, understanding, sympathy and kindness of the hon. member for Skeena would be $50,000. This is the cost to the taxpayers of having the hon. member for Skeena in parliament. This cost, of course, does not include the $10,000 which the hon. member receives annually. There are 265 members. If each member spoke at the same length as the hon. member for Skeena, the session would last 662 days per annum.

I will come to that, and I will come to you, too.
As I have said, this would mean 662 days per session, that is full days up to 10.30 at night. Even on the basis of six days a week, this would be equivalent to approximately 110 weeks a year, if all hon. members spoke as long as this very modest member for Skeena.
