125,000	at a cost of 40 cents per word. In other words the hon. member for Skeena, and it is his right to do it and in his wisdom he has done it, talks five times as much as the average member of parliament, as one can see from the number of pages of Hansard consumed.
Now, this results in delaying tactics. I suggest, with the greatest respect, that in some instances the delay is deliberate, and for no other purpose except to delay. I am not ascribing this to any member, I am not naming anyone. I have just been using an example for the purpose of illustration. I have been noting how some contributions by some members are constructive, and some contributions are not. In addition to this the hon. member for Skeena-we have to take some example and there is nothing personal about this-who insists on talking five times as long as the

average member, also insists that the average member should not have any extension of his time at six o'clock when we ask for five minutes or ten minutes to complete some item of business. The rules of the house enable the hon. member to call it six o'clock. As I say, these calculations do not include the time during which he was excluded.
Let us take another example. I am just picking these out of the hat. I refer now to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). Up to June 26, there were 7,103 pages in Hansard. The number of pages which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had filled amount to 276, so the percentage of the total number of pages of Hansard attributable to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was 3.8 per cent. The number of days which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would have filled if he had started talking at 11 o'clock in the morning and continued through until 10.30 at night is 5.3. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate made a contribution to parliament, therefore, which cost the Canadian taxpayer $106,000. This is the cost of keeping this precious flower in parliament. In addition, of course, he gets a nominal consideration of $10,000.
Now, if the average member of parliament spoke at the same length as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, every session of parliament would occupy four years. It must be obvious that the hon. member speaks twice as long as the hon. member for Skeena and about ten times as long as the average member of parliament. If he assessed his value to the house at twice as much as that of us ordinary mortals, I could understand it. Perhaps the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate considers himself and his contribution to be three times as valuable as the rest of us, or four or five times as valuable.
However, Mr. Speaker, I ask you with great humility-and at the moment my heart is full of humility-has any member, no matter how brilliant he may be and no matter where he comes from, no matter what regime he is representing in that pocket borough, particularly when he sits in opposition and has nothing to do with the business of the country except criticize it, the right to talk ten times as much as the average member? Now, you can give your own answer to that question. I am not going to suggest he has not because I know that he is highly esteemed in certain circles-particularly self-esteemed. I have heard from him about his greatness and his
The Budget-Mr. Roberge ability so often that I am sometimes convinced he perhaps has a right to talk longer than ordinary members. But not ten times longer.
This is my contribution to this budget debate. It is a pleasant one, a happy one and ends on a happy note. However, it might explain to the members of the house, Mr. Speaker, why we are here going through these dreary days and evenings; why as July 1 approaches we are here when we had contemplated that we were going to get home to our families and plan those things which since November last we have been prevented from doing; and why we are now promised with breaking all records and being in session longer than any other parliament. I say to you that "the fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars but in ourselves". That is where it lies. This speech is not political; it is factual. I obtained those figures from a statistician.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with as much care as possible to what the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) has just said. I am greatly surprised that a minister of the crown has taken about 25 minutes in participating in a budget debate and that, of those 25 minutes, he has used 15 minutes in criticizing other hon. members of this house, particularly the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). Even though he has statisticians to work for him, I would have thought that a minister of the crown would work on the statistics dealing with the economy of the country. I think the minister should also have told us that since 1960 we have been here in this house in this parliament for at least 15 out of a total of 18 months; and if the business of this nation during those 18 months was not carried out in less than 15 months it is on account of the mismanagement of the business of this house. He should have told us also that with respect to some measures on which everybody agreed those on this side of the house could have had many speakers. I have reference especially to the resolution with regard to increasing the pensions of veterans, and on which everyone was in agreement. The government had 48 speakers. (Translation):
Mr. Speaker, there are several conflicting theories on Canada's economy. There is the theory of cyclical budgeting, the theory of deficit budgeting and finally the theory of surplus budgeting.
It seems that the longer the speeches made by the present Minister of Finance, the
7202	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Roberge heavier the deficits. Apparently, it was necessary for the government to drown its incompetence and mismanagement in the flood of words spoken by the Minister of Finance on June 20 last.
Since 1957, when the present government was elected to office-that was four years ago-we have heard six budget speeches, though the Minister of Finance refers to his December 1957 budget as being only financial proposals.
Since 1958, or over a period of 3i years, five budget speeches were made by the Minister of Finance. Four of those budgets predicted deficits; only one forecast a surplus, that of March 31, 1960.
The December 1960 budget was labelled the baby budget. I am inclined to believe that the baby budget was rather that of March 31, 1960, but that the real budget, that was concealed at the time, was the budget brought down on December 20, 1960.
The $12 million surplus that the minister expected in March 1960 had turned into a $345 million deficit by December 1960. This represents a difference of $357 million, or a million a day, as pointed out by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer).
Mr. Speaker, if we look at what the present government has cost us since it accepted the responsibility of office, we find that there is a tremendous difference between what the Canadian taxpayers have to pay and what we have been told by various members in this house.
In 1957-58, a $38.5 million deficit; in 195859, a $609.5 million deficit; in 1959-60, a $413 million deficit; in 1960-61, a $345 million deficit. And with the $650 million deficit expected for the current year by the Minister of Finance, we have a grand total of $2,056 million.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this house I deal only with federal policy and not with provincial policy, with all due deference to my hon. friend for Roberval.
If we add to the last figure I mentioned the depletion of the unemployment insurance fund in the amount of $900 million, and of the national defence special fund which reached $165 million, we get a total of $3,121 million.

In the budget he presented on June 20, the Minister of Finance told us that each and every one of his budgets were aimed at solving current problems. In fact, here is what he said as reported on page 6639 of Hansard:
The circumstances attending each budget have differed from those associated with the others. Each was aimed to meet the financial and fiscal problems of its time. Tonight's budget is designed to meet Canada's present needs and difficulties.
Everyone will recall the electoral campaigns of 1957 and 1958. Everybody also will recall the promises made by the Prime Minister of Canada and his supporters, especially concerning unemployment.
One of the main problems facing this government ever since it took over is no doubt unemployment. During his electoral campaign, the Prime Minister spoke about it quite often. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
On rising for the first time to speak in this house I cannot but recall and repeat the words uttered by my late husband in his maiden speech in the twenty third parliament:
I enter on my duties here with a deep sense of humility, with the highest respect for this house and an earnest desire to do the best possible job

as the representative of my constituency of Kings of the province of Prince Edward Island, and of this great country of Canada.
It is also for me an honour and a challenge to be selected by my constituents to follow in the footsteps not only of my husband but also of his father who for many years represented Kings county in this chamber and the province of Prince Edward Island in the parliament of Canada. It is my desire and my intention to follow, as best I can, the course which they set.
I have mentioned, Mr. Speaker, my feelings of humility but I must also say that I am filled too with sentiments of deep gratitude, first, to the loyal friends of my husband and myself who so faithfully supported me in the difficulties and trials of recent months, and then to those members of the House of Commons who have greeted me so warmly and kindly as I take up my duties as a new member of parliament.
It is the custom for new members to refer in detail to their constituencies in their maiden speeches. It would indeed be easy for me to describe the beauties of Kings county, but because I am aware that this has been done often and well in this house I shall not at this time follow the familiar practice. I should like to say a few words, however, about some matters of particular significance to the economic life of my constituency and province.
Although I have long been interested in the development of Prince Edward Island I have watched with particular interest the events that followed the change of government in 1957 when my husband and three of his colleagues came to Ottawa as supporters of our distinguished Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker). Prince Edward Island-the smallest province in the dominion and the one with the narrowest base for provincial revenue-is extremely dependent on financial relations with the dominion government to provide the necessary level of services for our people. In these times when all governmental costs are rising a new attitude was required. It was, I think an awareness of this need which made such a great difference in Prince Edward Island and the maritimes generally after June, 1957. Our people were much impressed with the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant of which Prince Edward Island received $2,500,000 annually. This was by far the largest single grant ever received from Ottawa. Under the new dominion-provincial agreements the amount will be substantially larger and the benefits to the citizens of Prince Edward Island will be great.
In our province, where the basic industries are agriculture, fisheries and the tourist trade, transportation is tremendously important. The roads to resources program initiated by the

dominion government has given Prince Edward Island the greatest road building program in its history. It will account for 158 miles of pavement in my constituency of Kings county.
The roads to resources program and the camp site and picnic program, which is also a joint dominion-provincial program, have greatly benefited Kings county which until recently was much neglected as a tourist area. We look forward to an increased development of the tourist trade in our province. In this connection I cannot refrain from a word about the causeway, a subject of such great interest to my husband and his colleagues. I am in full agreement with what the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) said the other day and I join with my three colleagues in urging the minister to do everything possible to press forward this tremendous undertaking.
More and more tourists will be coming to Prince Edward Island. Statistics covering the last ten years reveal a sharp annual increase. The existence of new and improved facilities in the province and more and better roads will contribute to the greater importance of the tourist industry. Better markets for the excellent island products require better transportation facilities and it is my hope that this government, which has already done so much for our province, will provide for us the most up-to-date transportation facilities we have yet had.
Members of parliament are always interested in public works projects within their own constituencies. I recently travelled throughout Kings county to see at first hand some of the required projects which could be of assistance to our economy and especially to the fishing industry. In the last four years an impressive number of wharves, breakwaters and warehouses have been built which have resulted in great improvement.
Kings county is one of the important fishing areas in Canada and from time to time I shall urge upon the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) improvements and extensions of facilities to provide greater accommodation and security to our fishermen. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. lady on her maiden speech and suggest that she paid perhaps too much heed to the argument which has been put forward in this house very recently by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) who, I am sure, is trying to make all members of the house conscious of how much they are costing the taxpayer when they open their mouths.
There is very little I wish to say about the budget at this time because the budget 90205-6-455
The Budget-Mr. Fisher speech presents an opportunity to members to speak on almost any topic within the purview of House of Commons business. The subject I wish to address most of my time to today is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the report which was tabled today by the special committee on broadcasting.
Before I do so I should like to say, in relation to the budget, that one aspect of it has found a great deal of favour in the area that I represent. People involved in the pulp and paper industry are very pleased with the indication that the devaluation of the dollar will improve their position in terms of trade with the United States. However, I should like to underline a criticism that has been made in regard to this step in that direction. We are left with a very indefinite idea as to how this devaluation procedure is going to take place. If the devaluation which we have already had is merely a psychological drop and there is not going to be certain control and direction on the part of the government to maintain this difference between the Canadian and the United States dollar at some definite figure, we are going to be in a most difficult situation with respect to our basic industries.
It is very hard to know what is the right figure for the Canadian dollar, but the pulp and paper industry is the bellwether industry in Canada at the present time, especially in terms of export sales. When the Canadian dollar is below the United States dollar, there is a bit of pump priming in that industry both on its capital side and job creation side. I have no doubt at all that if the dollar is devalued below the United States dollar to the tune of five cents or six cents it will lead to the extension of pulp and paper plants and perhaps also the creation of completely new pulp and paper operations in northwestern Ontario.
However, we have not that kind of indication from the minister, and the value of the Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the United States dollar is a complete mystery at the present time. This situation seems to be too tentative and indefinite for the purposes of the basic economy in our regions. I suggest we must know just what the dollar is going to be pegged at. If this is not done I suggest we will have a further period of haze and doubt in the pulp and paper industry.
Perhaps it is almost blasphemous to refer to one of the kudos which was handed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) during this debate, but yesterday the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Campbell) made reference to something in an attempt to equate or draw analogies between our Saviour and the Minister of Finance. When one reaches a situation

The Budget-Mr. Fisher of such hyperbole as this, it behooves one to go very, very slowly. I keep looking over there, and have for some time, but am unable to see a halo. Somehow it does not seem to have manifested itself. It seems to me, however, that the hon. member for Stormont in going to such lengths to indicate what a marvellous minister of finance we have should have taken a lesson or two from the sermon on the mount himself and not been so harsh and severe in referring to the head of the Bank of Canada. After all, I am sure that an individual so close to someone who might deliver something similar to the sermon on the mount would not turn around and send the head of the Bank of Canada to jail. It seems to me that he is blind to all the advantages of having such a religious and halo-type figure close to him.

speechtext:
The hon. minister says he would like to be excused. I am not suggesting because I cannot see a halo that he is sprouting horns.
Today we had laid before this house the final report of the special committee on broadcasting. I should like to say immediately that I think it is a very unfair report which continues something that was very much in evidence two years ago when the committee met, and represents a very definite attempt on the part of certain members of that committee to do away with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I am not critical of their views, but of the method they used in developing those views. It seemed to me those members were more than suspicious of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, more than suspicious of the efficiency of that corporation, and more than suspicious about the way it carries out its programming. I believe they want to destroy the C.B.C. as a public corporation. I believe they would be happy to see the C.B.C. sold or disposed of through

some method. I believe they would like to see the C.B.C. completely detached from either programming or distribution, in other words, wiped out. Because this particular attitude of their does not have general support, they proceed on a course of niggling, nose punching, hammering and continually downgrading the organization as such. I should like to return to the report to indicate why I think this is so.
Does the hon. member wish to ask a question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question? He made a flat-footed statement about the attitude of members on the government side with respect to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and, as he says, of their desire to sell the corporation. Will he give us concrete proof of that?

speechtext: Otherwise he will be running away-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not running away. I am not saying that government members as a whole want to do this, but there are certain government members whose attitude toward the C.B.C. is completely destructive. I am saying that this report, like the report of two years ago, is a victory for this group. I am not saying they are a majority within the government party, but they are strong enough to get recommendations through that, I will argue, have no relation to the evidence that we heard and the investigation that was carried out this summer.
I should like to turn to one example which I think is the most serious of all, and it relates to recommendation No. 3, which reads:
That the number of directors of Canadian Broadcasting Corporation be increased from 11 to 15 for the purpose of assuring adequate representation to the French language network.
This is the part I have in mind:
That the directors be appointed on a rotating
basis-
This part is fine, but this is what I want to draw to the attention of the house:
-and a chairman be named from among their numbers by the governor in council for a period not to exceed five years. Further, that no executive officer or other employee of the corporation be a director of the corporation.
To me, Mr. Speaker, this is nothing more than a downgrading of the president of the C.B.C. to the role of manager. It means the elevation of the chairman of the board, as I conceive it, if this recommendation is carried out, to be the policy spokesman of the C.B.C. And yet it is very well argued-and I know the hon. member for Greenwood is an example-a member whom I respect tremendously-that this will be an improvement

because he can give examples of private corporations where such a situation existed. I believe this can do nothing but harm to the C.B.C. because of the role it plays in relation to the public. Who from now on, if this recommendation is accepted, is going to speak for the C.B.C.? Who is going to be the spokesman? The policy-making board will be detached from the executive officers in any real sense in so far as the operating is concerned; the operating officers will be detached from the board so far as policy is concerned. It seems to me, in a situation like this, you are going to create immense difficulties for the C.B.C. in achieving the kind of flexibility that is required of a public corporation that is always in the public eye and always under public criticism. It seems to me it robs it of the flexibility that it has under the present arrangement. There is one thing about it. The thing that really bothers me most about this recommendation, Mr. Speaker, is that the president of the C.B.C., Mr. Ouimet, a gentleman of whom I have been critical in some aspects of his work, made an excellent presentation before our committee for a period staggered over about three months. He did a magnificent job. I know if I were a French Canadian I would be particularly proud of the way in which this man from a French Canadian background, with a magnificent vocabulary and a great deal of information, marshalled and presented it to our committee. He handled himself splendidly in both languages and you felt that here was a person carrying on a magnificent job. I can only regret that through illness he was not available two years ago, at the time the C.B.C. was previously before our committee. As a result of that fine job he did in providing us with information and putting up with us for a day of examination and cross-examination, what does he get? A punch in the nose. He is going to be downgraded to something in the nature of a manager or general manager, and we are going to have a chairman over him.
It seems to me there is an inconsistency in this recommendation in that it does not indicate whether the appointment of the chairman by the governor in council is to be a part-time or a full-time appointment. We had the Auditor General give evidence before the committee in relation to the C.B.C. Some members of the committee seemed to be very impressed with his evidence in certain sectors. Here was an instance where the Auditor General felt that if we were to have a chairman of the C.B.C. he should be a full-time person, but for some reason the committee did not take this into account. It seems to me 90205-6-455i
The Budget-Mr. Fisher the recommendation makes sense only if this is a full time appointment.
We have to accept the fact that Mr. Ouimet has been punched in the nose or given his little bit of punishment; I do not know for what reason. But you must have someone speaking for the C.B.C. full time. In an organization of this scope which deals with day to day problems which are cropping up all the time which affect policy, how can you have a part-time person in this kind of role? Certainly the Auditor General, if you respect the advice he had to give, felt that it should be a full-time appointment. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, as I say, I interpret this as another punch in the nose for the C.B.C. and particularly for the president of the C.B.C. who came forward and gave evidence.
To me the real irony in all this is that after Mr. Henderson, the Auditor General, gave his evidence suggesting a management consultant should examine the C.B.C., after he had made his recommendation about a fulltime chairman of the board, the committee asked, as a result of a motion that I introduced, which was supported generally, that we bring Mr. Dunsmore before the committee, who is I suppose what you might call the acting chairman of the board. I would like to point out that Mr. Dunsmore is an appointee of this government. He came before us and gave evidence for a considerable length of time. Every member had an opportunity to question him. It was not a case of his dodging in and dodging out. In his testimony at which I should like all members who are interested in the problem to look-* it appears in the minutes of proceedings and evidence No. 27-he gave no indication that the board of directors was satisfied with things in the C.B.C., but he did point out to us, and in his evidence showed, that he had a great deal of business experience, and his associates on the board, particularly the finance committee, had a great deal of experience. They are not rubes; they are not duds. They were appointed by this government. Did he give any indication anywhere that they wanted this kind of recommendation? Not a bit of it. You cannot find anywhere in the evidence here that the chairman of the board appointed by this government felt that the board was not operating well. You cannot find any evidence at all that I can see that can be brought forward to indicate that Mr. Dunsmore felt the corporation was not operating well. I challenged him with the question, is the C.B.C. a bad corporation from the point of view of efficiency? He said he certainly did not think so, or words to that effect. To me he gave an affirmation in the performance of the corporation and the

The Budget-Mr. Fisher role of the board. And here we are, without any support from this particular group whose spokesman we had before us, with this recommendation from a parliamentary committee that no executive officer or other employee of the corporation be a director of the corporation.
Well, Mr. Speaker, in regard to this kind of attack on the C.B.C. let me say this. I have never been critical, and never could be as an individual, of any member of parliament who wants to say his piece in public about what he believes in relation to any organization over which the government has any control. All I can say is that if a member believes that the C.B.C. should go, if he believes that it should be doing just programming or just handling the distribution of programs, if he believes that it no longer has a role to play; that private enterprise or private stations and private networks can do the job, then he should come forward and make that point and not proceed by this process of niggling, cutting away and undermining.
I will give another example to indicate what I mean by this undermining in the committee report. As many members know, the C.B.C. has most of its production facilities in Toronto and Montreal. In Montreal these facilities are scattered in over 20 places and in Toronto in over 12. A great deal of cost is involved in terms of communication and transportation. Anyone who visits the various Toronto headquarters cannot help but be overwhelmed by the expensive crazy quilt setup. The C.B.C., it seems to me quite properly, had plans to consolidate these facilities and had a capital investment program in relation thereto. Paragraph 6 in the committee report reads, in part:
Your committee commends the caution of the board of directors in its policy toward large capital investments at this time in Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa.
What the committee is commending is the information Mr. Dunsmore gave us that the board is seized of the changes and transitional effects with regard to broadcasting at this time and, therefore, is not going to rush into anything. In other words, the people the government appointed were aware of the situation. The committee then recommends that this course be pursued until all studies and investigations are completed. Well, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me the committee is underlining again the fact that it does not really feel the board of directors who are directing the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are in control of things. I am prepared to accept Mr. Dunsmore's assurance that the board is watching these matters very carefully. Apparently the other members of the committee-they have this right because they are


in the majority-do not feel this way. We have, therefore, a suggestion going out again that the C.B.C., which desperately needs expansion of these facilities in Montreal and Toronto in order to consolidate because of the extra cost involved, is given an O.K., to delay, postpone and procrastinate. This spirit, on occasion, is ideal because of the changing television situation. However, it seems to me there is an attitude of, damned if we are going to allow the C.B.C. to consolidate any more.

The hon. member is quite aware of the fact that I helped to bring out, by the questioning of Mr. Dunsmore, the position that is involved. I am willing to leave it to the board of directors. I seem to be the only member of the committee who has faith in the appointments made by this government.
Another kind of niggling which is involved in this report, Mr. Speaker, is illustrated by paragraph No. 8. This paragraph reads:
There Is evidence to indicate that the supervision and control of scripts and programming has not reached the levels envisaged in the recommendations made by the broadcasting committee of 1959.
There is a honey, Mr. Speaker. I do not know what it was that was envisaged by the broadcasting committee of 1959. I do not know what the evidence is to indicate that the supervision and control of scripts and programming has not reached the levels envisaged in the recommendations made by the broadcasting committee of 1959. This recommendation really does not say anything, except to indicate again that somehow there is something haywire with C.B.C. scripts and programming. If hon. members feel that C.B.C. programming is far afield, if they feel the C.B.C. is getting into what an hon. member from Newfoundland called a lot of subversive stuff, if as other members charged the C.B.C. is dealing too much with indelicate matters such as in the Zoo Story, dealing with homosexuality and other immoral things, why do they not say so? No, they say there is evidence to indicate that supervision and control of scripts and programming has not reached the levels envisaged in the recommendations made by the broadcasting committee of 1959.
Then, the committee, in turn, recommends that every effort be made by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to exert a stricter

control in this field of public information and entertainment. What are these things of which we want stricter control? What do we want to do, keep more people off the air? What kind of programming is it that is so bad that we need stricter control? Is there something immoral, indecent, improper or subversive in the general level of C.B.C. programs and scripts?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have stated repeatedly, Mr. Speaker, and I state again that I am a strong supporter of the C.B.C. However, it seems to me obvious that there are programs on the C.B.C. which deeply offend a large number of people in this country. I do feel that it is desirable, although I know it is difficult, that more scrutiny be given to these programs.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to ask the hon. member who has put that question, how could you have freedom for the producers and writers if you are always going to be calling for stricter control? Our evidence did not reveal anywhere that there was any crisis or anything seriously wrong in this field. If the hon. member will look back he will find that any broadcasting organization that is doing any kind of job in the field of public information and entertainment is going to be rubbing the feelings of some people the wrong way. I am a politician, and I want to get along with people, particularly the people in my constituency. However, I am always rubbing some people the wrong way. There are two other points which bother me that I wanted to comment upon in relation to this report. These are omissions. There are two that are important, and one I cannot fathom. In 1959, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was urged by a parliamentary committee to do what the Fowler commission recommended, that is to have a more aggressive commercial policy.
We received evidence before the committee to a degree that this commercial policy is having effects upon the C.B.C. staff, and upon its relationship with private stations or its competition with private stations. The C.B.C. brought forward the idea that was recommended by the Fowler commission, namely that it be put on some kind of financial basis that had a formula, that was not dependent upon what took place each year when it came before treasury board. I do not know what happened. We had opinions from the Auditor General. We had evidence from the C.B.C. However, in the report there is nothing about that matter. There is in it not a thing about this very difficult question of a commercial policy of the C.B.C.
I should like to make it perfectly clear that a couple of years ago I and our party were against the C.B.C. going out further into commercial operations. However, it is now out there. It is now doing the chore, and commercial revenue is becoming more

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while in this budget debate it is open to any hon. member to speak about any of the activities of the government of Canada or about anything which is of interest to parliament and while we have listened, I think, with interest and profit to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who has just delivered what might be called a provocative speech, in the few minutes available to me I propose to confine myself to observations on some of the financial proposals made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in the budget address.
Before I do that, however, I should like to welcome to the house the four new members, in particular the hon. member for Kings (Mrs. Macdonald) who so graciously addressed the House of Commons earlier this afternoon and also the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) who is a friend of mine of 15 years' standing and for whom I have especially tender feelings. Thirteen years ago he and I walked the floor of the Toronto General hospital together on a spring afternoon awaiting the arrival of his first son and my only daughter. It seems to me that at that time we were talking politics, Mr. Speaker. Since that time we have had a very friendly relationship although disagreeing entirely on political questions. I should also like to say this, and I hope it will not be terribly embarrassing to the hon. gentleman to whom I refer. I think that the government and Canadians generally are greatly indebted to the distinguished Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). I have known this hon. gentleman for some 13 years. Over that time I have watched his service to our party and to the country. I have admired the diligent way in which he has conducted himself and the great efforts he has put forward to serve his minister and his country. About his minister I shall have something to say in a few minutes.
The purpose of the budget proposals put forward by the minister was to help to create in this country conditions which would give rise to greater employment and steady and sensible growth in the Canadian economy. One of the standards by which our kind of society is judged is the success or otherwise we have in providing jobs for people who desire to work. In my opinion in North America recently we have not come up to a particularly high standard in this respect. When the budget proposals are implemented and when the effects of many of the other measures passed by this parliament are felt, I think we can look forward to a gradual increase in employment opportunities in this country.

Related to expanding employment is the objective of promoting growth in the economy. A mix of reforms, monetary, fiscal and economic, are before the house for consideration and I think that each of these in its own way should be helpful. In the next few minutes I intend to speak briefly about certain developments in the Canadian economy which have had an adverse effect on its growth in recent years and to indicate how I think the proposals put forward by the Minister of Finance may arrest these developments. These developments do not fit into any geometric pattern and one cannot speak with certainty as to the effects they have had or as to the results the budget proposals may have by way of providing solutions to some of these problems. In some respects they are related to each other and in other respects they are not related. They have different causes. Some economists refer to these developments as cyclical, structural and technological, but I do not propose to use these terms. I think that Canadians generally are becoming aware of what these developments are, but I do not think it is yet clear enough that in the 1960's we have quite a different kind of situation within Canada and the world of the 1960's is drastically different from the world of the 1950's.
Of course, one of the factors which has had an important effect on Canadian business is the strengthening of the economies of the countries of western Europe and the resurgence of the economy of Japan. Earlier this year I had an opportunity to see something of this industrial development in Japan and I was terribly impressed by the zeal, drive, enthusiasm and acumen of the Japanese businessmen whom I met. In Europe it is becoming more and more difficult to sell our goods because the countries of that continent are becoming increasingly more capable of satisfying their own needs.
In the case of the western European countries an important impetus was given to industrial expansion after the war by the Marshall plan, and in the case of Japan by United States economic assistance. Developments in these countries have tended to slow down some business activity in Canada, but in the long term I think they will be helpful to Canada. A healthy European economy is needed by our country, which looks to European markets for export trade.
It has been suggested that something akin to the Marshall plan is now required in the less developed areas of Asia and Africa to give them the capital required for a take-off similar to that displayed by the western European countries in the 1950's. I do not think the analogy is a particularly good one, but certainly capital investment in these
The Budget-Mr. Stinson areas will help them get into a position where they will be better able to purchase Canadian goods. Many of the budget proposals will help Canadian indusry to become more competitive, especially, in my opinion, those designed to bring down the exchange rate, reduce interest rates and those having to do with research carried on in Canada.
May I turn, second, to the question of the balance of payments. This is an extremely complex and difficult field. On June 20 the minister told us that in the past five years we have had net inflows of capital from outside of from $1 billion to $1,500,000,000 each year. Each year the value of goods and services we have bought outside the country has exceeded the value of goods and services we have sold to others. It has been said by some that this shows Canadians are living beyond their means. Certainly it would be a good thing if Canada had all the capital required for developing our own resources, and it would be to our advantage if we had a favourable balance on current international account. But the fact is that now, and for as long one can see into the future, it is going to be necessary for this country to borrow money abroad to develop our resources.
Surely it is obvious that United States investment has been one of the main reasons for our post-war prosperity, and as I say we are going to require and welcome investment by financial institutions in that country for a long time. As to the surplus of exports over imports, it seems to me that this is a problem more easily corrected than that arising from foreign borrowings. At least it is a field where individual Canadian purchasers may help out by wherever possible purchasing Canadian goods and services.
To help correct the imbalance of payments the government proposes to use the exchange stabilization fund. The minister said that the fund would be used "to neutralize, at least to some degree, the effects of the continuing capital inflows". To make any significant change in the rate there would have to be very heavy buying of United States dollars out of this fund, and the minister himself has recognized that the advantage that can be expected by using this technique is very limited because of the huge sums of money which would have to be expended to make any really significant change in the rate.
It seems to me that more important are the government's proposals to encourage borrowings within Canada. Anyone who has had any connection with the financing of capital works of the municipality of metropolitan Toronto will know how dependent that municipality has been on borrowings from the United States to finance its program. It is
7212	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Stinson the hope of the government that to a greater extent than before municipalities such as that will be able to find in Canada the resources they need for their capital undertakings.
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes left to me I should like to say something about the co-operation asked for by the minister between government and secondary industry, and in particular about the proposal for expansion of the activities of the industrial development bank. The industrial development bank can be of limited help to secondary industry generally in this country, but it can be of some help, and unless we see greater opportunities for employment in the manufacturing industries of this country we are going to be looking at unemployment figures of something like 7 per cent to 10 per cent of the labour force for a long time to come. I do not believe these figures are acceptable to the Canadian people. In the European countries there has been intimate co-operation among government, labour and management. It seems to me that this kind of co-operation is something that has to be fostered and encouraged by each of these three groups.
I think the work of the national productivity council can be helpful in this regard. In that connection I think it was unfortunate that there were not appointed to that body younger men who have more time to devote to the work of the council than its present members. The members of that council are big names; they are great Canadians in their own fields, but they are too busy to be expected to carry on the amount of important work which that council should do. I can think of a number of young Canadian businessmen who are anxious to serve their country. They are well informed and experienced in their fields and they have not yet had an opportunity to serve their country on a council of this kind.
With regard to the industrial development bank, it seems to me that the managers of the branches of that bank have to start to get more in tune with businessmen who are coming to them with loan applications. I think, also, they have to start to show something of the sense of urgency which we find shown by managers of the large branches of the chartered banks when dealing with applications for loans from the businessmen among their customers. I would like to see some of these people show some of the same kind of drive and enthusiasm which we see displayed these days by the distinguished Minister of Finance. Speaking of that honourable gentleman, I would like to say that I consider him a man of steel, a skilful parliamentarian, a leader of men and one of the great Canadians of our time.


Another field where the government is showing initiative in assisting manufacturers is in the field of tariffs and quotas. Under this administration many sections of the tariff have been revised and at all times the government has fulfilled this country's obligations under the GATT. The quota arrangements recently completed with Japan have relieved to some extent the concerns of Canadian manufacturers of radio sets and tubes. While I know the negotiations have been delicate and difficult-and the Minister of Finance is to be congratulated on a reasonably good result

I sometimes think the government shows undue concern over a country such as Japan cutting down on its purchases of Canadian wheat. There are no price supports on unused tubes and resistors and no public money is used to pay storage bills on the inventories of the electronic and electrical industry. I think these facts should be kept in mind when the government is considering the position of farmers and other Canadian citizens in the course of these trade negotiations.

speechtext:
Toward the end of his budget speech the Minister of Finance said that this budget challenges all people to hard work and self-discipline. It is trite but none the less true to say that governments cannot make this a prosperous country. The Canadian nation will be prosperous if Canadians work hard and exercise those old virtues of being resourceful and exercising self-control. Earlier in the year there was a round of salary increases in my municipality for public officials who were already well paid, and the thought came to my mind: Why should these people be asking for and receiving substantial increases in their pay for this year when they are doing no more work this year than last year? The answer to this question, of course, is that they should not have asked for or received more money. As the minister has said so often, for people who have a good rate of pay there is no justification for a pay increase unless there is a matching increase in productivity.
I do not think we should work in parliament or elsewhere for prosperity for Canada alone. Hon. members know that I am an advocate of foreign economic aid. One of the reasons I would like to see all Canadian workers employed is that then we would have more resources with which to help the economic development of less advanced countries. While some of the problems confronting us in the Canadian economy are difficult and baffling, they look comparatively unimportant when set alongside the difficulties facing the emerging nations in Africa and

Asia. I wish we could send our excellent Minister of Finance to help them out. He is giving great leadership to Canadians in these exciting days and he has earned the respect of statesmen throughout the world.

He said then, in a speech which was probably well delivered because it was well written:
In the field of textiles, the minister explained, history proves that the Conservatives have always been leaders in government action designed to protect this basic industry. Apart from helping to set up one of the first textile unions in Canada, the Conservative party has constantly sought to protect this industry. The Budget-Mr. Boulanger Let me quote a few figures. Since last year, cotton imports from the United States have risen by 240 million yards. It is the first time in Canadian history that we imported more cotton than we manufactured.
From 1954 to 1960, Japanese imports jumped from $4 million to $41 million. From 1958 to last year, imports from Hong Kong jumped from $3 to $10 million.
General imports from Japan increased by approximately 170 per cent.
I could have told him also that since the Conservative party took over, some 30 textile industries have closed down in Ontario and Quebec.
I could have told him that only this past year 900 workers have lost their job.
I have here a pamphlet from the primary textile industry association which has its headquarters in Montreal. Here are a few paragraphs from that pamphlet:
The demand for Canadian textile in 1970 would secure jobs for some 110,000 workers only, someone stated at the special Senate committee on manpower and employment on February 23, 1961.
The only hope of substantially increasing the present number of some 74,000 workers employed in the Canadian textile industry would be to replace imports by domestically made products, says a brief of the primary textile institute. We have to choose between imports and jobs.
The 33 page brief, signed by the chairman of the board, Mr. George H. Dobbie, and by the president, Mr. W. M. Berry, says: The rapidly growing labour force in Canada will need more jobs. While lucrative jobs are commendable objectives, no doubt they must be created to a certain degree within the professions where they are supplied in suificient number in comparison with investments and sales.
That study prepared by an outstanding economist shows that the manpower natural growth is such that within the next five years we shall have to provide jobs for one million more workers. That represents 200,000 new jobs a year until 1965. In 1960, only half that number has been provided.
That shows that there is a backlog in the creation of 200,000 new jobs a year.
I should like to tell the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion) that textile manufacturers are not satisfied with the result of discussions held with regard to the establishment of quotas on goods imported from Japan.
Indeed, in certain sectors, quotas have been increased, while in others they have been cut down.
Quotas on blouses and shirts have gone up by 3 per cent for 1961 shipments.


The quotas on knitted goods have been increased by 10 per cent.
There was a decrease for other goods, such as table linen, ranging about 10 per cent. There was also a reduction of 10 per cent in the case of knitted goods of textile fibre, etc. But on the whole, imports from Japan have not been reduced as much as we would have liked in the interests of the textile industry.
A greater number of jobs could have been provided in Quebec and in Ontario where 80 per cent of those industries are located.
Mr. Speaker, other basic industries will be affected as well. I refer particularly to the shoe industry. I would have liked the Secretary of State also to mention that primary industry of the province of Quebec.
In 1956, two and a half million pairs of canvas shoes were manufactured in Canada. In 1960, we were importing 69 per cent of our requirements in that field.
In 1956, we were importing a million pairs of rubber shoes; in 1960, we imported 4,750,000 pairs or 36.8 per cent of our requirements.
As far as electronics is concerned, a report handed out to the Prime Minister and to all the members gives figures indicating that before long, electronics will have disappeared from this country.
In 1956, we had 28 electronics plants. In 1960, only 18 of these remained.
From 1955 to 1959, the number of jobs in that industry went down by 28 per cent. I am told that there was another substantial decrease in 1960.
Imports of radios started when the Conservative party came to power in 1957.
In fact, in 1956, we were not importing radios. We imported 69,000 in 1957; 156,000 in 1958; 395,000 in 1959 and 692,000 in 1960, that is 77 per cent of the Canadian demand.
Besides creating unemployment, those imports made us lose revenues resulting from sales and excise taxes. In fact, in 1959, we lost on radios, $750,000 worth of taxes which we would otherwise have had if those radios had been made in Canada.
This is how it works. The 11 per cent sales tax and the 15 per cent excise tax apply on the basis of $20.35 for a radio made in Canada whereas for a similar 6-transistor radio made in Japan, those two taxes apply only on $13.20, which means a difference of $1.87 in

the yield of those two taxes. If this figure is multiplied by the number of imported sets, we get a total of $750,000 for 1959 and $1.3 million for 1960.
The Canadian electronic appliance manufacturers association made recommendations to which I give full support.
The first one is to eliminate the excise tax of 15 per cent on products from our industries.
Second, to limit imports to 10 per cent of the sales of our industries.
Third, to use the same valuation for purposes of taxation in the case of imported products as in the case of Canadian products.
If we turn now to the situation of the electronic tube industry, we find that in 1956, no electronic tubes were imported from Japan. In 1960, we imported $3.9 million worth of these tubes at a price of 29 cents each, that is 45.6 per cent of the total Canadian production. That means that we are now producing only 54.4 per cent of our needs, when in 1956 we were producing 100 per cent.
United States imports amount to only 1.7 per cent of their total production, while ours represent nearly 45.6 per cent of our requirements.
This means a lesser number of workers in electronics. In fact, between January 1, 1959 and October 31, 1960, there was a reduction of 34.5 per cent.
The federal treasury also suffered a heavy loss of revenues derived from excise and sales taxes, owing to those price differentials and the disappearance of our Canadian industries.
The recommendations submitted by the electronic tube industry association were the same as the ones put forward by the Canadian electronic industry association.
Recently, following an exchange of correspondence with the Canadian General Electric Company Limited, I received a letter dated November 30, 1960 over the signature of Mr. A. F. Johnston in which the latter made very appropriate observations on the electronic tube industry in Canada. He said, among other things:
Today, the electronic tube industry and the Canadian people are faced with serious problems arising from the imports from Japan of certain types of electronic tubes. In 1956, no such tubes were imported. We figure, however, that those imports will reach 5.7 million units for the year 1960, that is 45.6 per cent of the total Canadian production. Those figures illustrate the serious disruption caused by those imports to our Canadian production.
That situation only makes worse the ills already affecting the electronic industry and the whole of Canada.

I could speak at length on the question of revenue and farmers in this country, but I have a few words to say about the Canadian wheat board. I am not critical of the Canadian wheat board because it has played a role in the past and will in the future. I agree with the statement of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Milligan) who said on April 11, 1961-and he should be commended because 1 feel he knew what he was talking about and spoke in a consistent and intelligent way. He said:
I surely agree that the grain commission is doing an excellent job concerning the sale of grain. I think we have there an example of planned marketing which has proved to be good. My only wish is that we could apply the same marketing system to a number of other products because then agriculture would not be in its present bad situation.


And the hon. member went on to say that the wheat board was a fine organization. I readily endorse his remarks. However, I might ask what the Canadian wheat board has done to help eastern farmers, especially last fall.
When the estimates of the Department of Agriculture were under consideration, I talked about the Canadian wheat board and more particularly about the losses incurred last fall by eastern farmers with regard to the delivery and the prices of feed grain. Last fall feed grain was hard to get and when we succeeded in getting some, we had to pay quite a high premium. The reason was that the Canadian wheat board had no authority to store grain for the milling of feed for eastern farmers. This matter was dealt with at length during consideration of the Canadian wheat board report which was concluded yesterday.
I must say at this stage that I was most disappointed to notice that few members of the province of Quebec attended the four meetings of that committee. In fact, there was only one Conservative member and he stayed only an hour.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after having trespassed upon the patience of the house at very great length in introducing the budget on June 20, it is with some diffidence that I rise now to conclude the debate on the main opposition amendment. However, Mr. Speaker, I say in extenuation of this circumstance that, under the rules, this is the last opportunity that I have to speak in the budget debate or offer a reply to anything that has been said in the debate up to this point.
I thank those hon. members who have spoken in this debate, and especially those who have spoken in a kindly fashion about the budget. May I say that the reception accorded the budget generally throughout the country has been unusually favourable and is indeed very gratifying. It is evident that the country welcomes the broad and comprehensive program of constructive action put forward in the budget. Today, Mr. Speaker, by reason of the limitation of time I must confine myself to several points that have

The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming
been raised in the discussion by hon. members of the opposition who have spoken. In coming to those various matters, of which I shall be discussing several, may I ask hon. members to consider first what are the results of the budget as visible to date in the eight days that have passed since its delivery.
First of all, in regard to the exchange rate on the Canadian dollar, which measures the external value of the dollar and not its internal value in terms of domestic transactions in Canada, may I say that in keeping with the purpose of the budget the Canadian dollar has moved to a discount of approximately 3 per cent in terms of the United States dollar.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At the moment only by talk. We will see.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will have to ask the hon. member to control himself because time is limited and I am trying to conclude my remarks so that there may be an earlier vote, which I understand is the wish of hon. members opposite.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, a considerable measure of stability has been developed which I think is very gratifying. The next observation, Mr. Speaker, has been the view taken by the financial markets of this country in the eight days that have passed. It must be, in the light of the alarm sounded by hon. members opposite, gratifying that in the eight days that have intervened since the budget the financial markets of this country are stronger than they were before the budget was introduced.

If the hon. member is going to persist, then I am not going to be able to finish in time as I was endeavouring to do. I shall have to deal with these silly and misleading interjections. It rests entirely with him.
In all categories of Canadian bonds, short, medium and long term, the fact is that these Canadian issues are stronger now than they were when the budget was introduced. Correspondingly, the interest yields on these bonds in the market today has been reduced accordingly. I think this is a very good test of the degree of confidence engendered in the government's financial program in the appraisal to which the country has submitted it.
I now come to these specific criticisms. The tenor of observations of hon. members opposite has revolved around first, the reduction in the external value of the Canadian dollar; second, the deficit; and third, the danger, as they see it, of inflation. Let me
say that while I propose to reply to their observations, it is not because they put them forward with any semblance of a constructive approach. Indeed, the observations of hon. members opposite on these subjects have been singularly unproductive of ideas or proposals. Indeed, I think it not unfair to say that hon. members opposite have avoided suggesting solutions like the plague.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Last year and the year before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is up to the hon. member.
Let me speak now about what hon. members say with regard to the dollar. Their criticism has been harsh. They have viewed the decline in the external value of the Canadian dollar by these three percentage points with fear and foreboding. There has been a great confusion on the part of hon. members opposite, a cacophony of discordant and contradictory voices. I take you back very briefly, Mr. Speaker, to the national Liberal convention of December last. It was stated there, and it has been stated elsewhere by what were thought to be authoritative voices in the Liberal party, that this party opposite wanted a lower exchange value for the Canadian dollar. It is commonly understood that Mr. Walter Gordon, who is regarded as a very important spokesman for the Liberal party on financial questions, favoured this course. He was chairman of the resolutions committee of the Liberal national convention. What has Mr. Gordon been saying? He has been reasonably consistent on this subject. On March 17, 1961, he stated:
We need instead an expansionist approach to economic policy: easier credit, lower interest rates and a lower exchange rate for the dollar.
Again, we have Mr. Gordon saying this on June 5, 1961. He decries what he calls the tight money policy and then he goes on to say this:
The government should state its firm intention to see that the present artificially high exchange rate for the Canadian dollar is reduced in order to stimulate business activity in Canada.
This should be brought about by the proposed changes in monetary policy and reduction in interest rates, coupled with skilful operation of the foreign exchange fund. However, if in the opinion of the authorities more direct action would be needed in addition to accomplish some measure of devaluation, they-
Meaning the government.
-should not hesitate to take it.
Mr. Speaker, these are the things we have proposed in the budget. These are the things that hon. members opposite are criticizing. May I say that I will take Walter Gordon's opinion before I will take the opinion on
7218	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming such questions of any hon. members opposite who have spoken in this debate.
Here is Mr. Gordon on this same occasion again on June 5. He states:
But at present much of our own resources are idle and unemployment, not inflation, is the main problem that confronts us.
I ask hon. members opposite to bear that in mind when I come back to that theme. Again here is a report on that Liberal meeting, the meeting of Liberal minds in Kingston last September. It is a report in the Ottawa Journal of September 7, 1960. Here we have a reference to Mr. Gordon's statement there:
The best immediate step to assist such industries he thought would be in reducing the present high value of the Canadian dollar.
Here we have a report of January 10, 1961, reporting on the Liberal national convention. They are advocating lower interest rates to remove the premium on the Canadian dollar. Again, here is the Toronto Telegram of January 10, 1961, reporting a speech made at the convention by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). This is what he advocates:
Maintain, through a "flexible monetary policy", lower dollar exchange rates to aid both the tourist industry and export trade.
Again here we have, on January 11, 1961, another report from that convention:
New monetary policies would stimulate exports and improve Canada's position by lowering the value of the Canadian dollar.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members opposite cannot have it both ways. They have turned their backs on what was said at the convention. That is only five months ago. They have thrown the convention platform overboard if they mean what they have been saying in this debate so far on this subject, and it is evident they have thrown overboard what Mr. Gordon has been saying, presumably on their behalf. They have repudiated their platform in this regard. They have repudiated Mr. Gordon.
We say that this movement of the Canadian dollar to this present position is going to aid trade, to aid employment and to aid in redressing the imbalance in our international payments. In this respect the policy of this budget is a continuation of the same policy that was put forward before the house in the two budgets introduced in 1960. Following the budget of March 31, 1960 there was a reduction in the external value of the Canadian dollar. Following the supplementary budget of December 20, 1960 there was a further reduction. This present budget carries further the same progress. This budget is completely in accord with the purposes of those two budgets of 1960.


I pass now to the next subject which has engaged the attention of hon. members opposite. They complain about the deficit. They see no virtue in the deficit that has been proposed in this budget. They picture the country as going to blue ruin because of this deficit.
It is a large deficit admittedly, Mr. Speaker. It could have been reduced. I could have recommended to the house a budget that would have contemplated a smaller deficit. I could, for instance, have proposed that there would not be any tax reductions. We would have had a smaller deficit if I had not proposed tax reductions. We would have had a smaller deficit if we had not proposed to increase the benefits to veterans in the form of pensions and allowances at this session. Do hon. members opposite wish to see the deficit reduced by denying those pensions and allowance increases to the veterans? My colleague the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) this afternoon reminded us that in the aid this government has given to the provinces and their institutions since we came into office we have moved up, as compared with the last fiscal year before we came into office, the payments to or for the benefit of the provinces from $690 million in that year to $1,470 million in this year. Is it any wonder that we have a deficit? The deficit has arisen by reason of the tremendous increase we have made in these payments to and for the benefit of the provinces. These are transfer payments.
Hon. members opposite cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. They talked out of both sides of their mouths throughout this debate. This is not a new tactic. They proposed deficit financing at their convention and they have been saying the same thing since then. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) will not mind if I remind him of a report in the Toronto Daily Star of last September in which he is reported as saying that he would not favour deficit budgeting in normal times. He was asked if these were normal times and he said no, that they are not normal times. He is on record elsewhere. Here he is at the Liberal convention last January proposing a deficit. He calls it a planned deficit. Ours is certainly a planned deficit.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a result of deliberate policies and decisions. Make no mistake about that fact, Mr. Speaker. The Leader of the Opposition has advocated deficit financing for times like these. However, it seems that his followers believe in deficits when Liberals bring them in but that they

do not believe in deficits in these circumstances when a Conservative government brings them in. That is the difference.
Do not take my word for it, Mr. Speaker. I have here a statement made last week by Dr. Donald E. Armstrong of McGill University, in a speech he made over the radio. He was speaking first of all about the program proposed by the governor of the Bank of Canada in the statement he put out a week ago Monday, June 19; that is the one that had been sent to me in confidence last February. Of it he says this:
But judged on its key recommendations, the Coyne budget is just sheer nonsense. The idea of balancing a budget and increasing taxes in order to fight a recession is ridiculous. As far as I am concerned the Coyne budget has shown me that Mr. Coyne's area of incompetence extends far beyond monetary policy, and that he is equally badly informed on matters of trade and fiscal policy.
And further:
Mr. Coyne is really only the chief propagandist of bad economics. He has achieved that position partly because he is a forceful and persuasive speaker, and partly because he has control of the central bank's propaganda machinery which enables him to spread his nonsense effectively at the expense of the taxpayer.
And further:
Against this back drop of stagnation, how does the budget look? To me it looks just fine. In its total effects it is very much what the country needs.
And further:
A $1 billion cash deficit is just about what the economy needs to lengthen and strengthen the upswing. The cash deficit is a measure of the additional spending power which is being pumped into the economy. Provided that it is accompanied by an appropriate monetary policy, this additional spending will be translated into additional employment.
Mr. Speaker, that is what we have in mind and that is what we have proposed to the house in asking the approval of the house. Hon. members opposite will have their opportunity of being judged by what they have said in this debate or the things they have said outside which are contradictory of the things they have said in this house.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) -if he does not mind my reminding him of what he said in the T.V. press program last Thursday night-said, speaking of what would have happened if he had been leading the government at this time, "We would have had a deficit too". So, Mr. Speaker, hon. members opposite who have been critical of the deficit apparently have decided to repudiate what has been said on their behalf by their leader and elsewhere.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the minister has quoted me. I know he would like to quote me accurately and I dislike interrupting him, but he stated that
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming I said we would have had a deficit. What I said in this broadcast was that we would have had a deficit in 1958, when we were in a recession; but now, according to the minister, we are not in a recession any longer.

Does the Leader of the Opposition say now that he would not be budgeting for a deficit if he were doing the budgeting today? If he does say that, Mr. Speaker, he is contradicting what the Liberal national convention proposed and he is contradicting what Mr. Walter Gordon has been saying. Here is what Mr. Walter Gordon said on June 5, 1961, and here he was laying out in his speech at Simcoe his proposals for the coming budget:
The Minister of Finance will be budgeting for yet another deficit, and it is difficult to see how, in the circumstances, any over-all reduction in taxes could be justified at this time. This is particularly true if the authorities really believe, as the Prime Minister suggested in a recent speech, that the end of the recession is in sight. In fact, if the authorities expect a substantial improvement in business conditions in the near future, some increases in taxation even may be called for.
Are hon. members opposite calling for increases in taxes? Well, Mr. Coyne did. He called for increases in personal income taxes; he called for increases in corporation taxes, indeed such a rate of increase in corporation taxes as would have set back recovery in this country perhaps very seriously; he called for increases in tariffs on everything coming into the country; he called for a federal gasoline tax, and other things.
These are the contributions to the solution of our existing problems that hon. members opposite appear to be advocating. So far as I am aware, hon. members opposite have chosen to ignore what has been said in the budget speech; the concrete proposals for dealing with the problem of maintaining confidence and strengthening the financial markets. They have not been saying very much about the constructive proposals put forward here with regard to providing a purchase fund so that $100 million may be available this year for purchases of bonds in the open market to strengthen that market, particularly the medium and long term end of it. They have not said anything about the constructive proposal to remove the overhang upon the market in the form of the securities held by the unemployment insurance fund. They have not said anything

The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming about the constructive proposals we have put forward in regard to the marketing of new issues. They have chosen to ignore these.
They have chosen instead to try to break down confidence and make the country think that we are in for a horrible experience of inflation. That leads me, Mr. Speaker, to say this. They are talking as though the finances of this country are in a shaky condition. Mr. Speaker, I ask leave of the house at this point, in trying to save time, to put on the record figures that have been taken from official government records calculating the net debt per capita in this country in the years 1950 to 1961 and as a percentage of gross national product. May I have leave, Mr. Speaker?

My third subject, Mr. Speaker, is inflation. Hon. members opposite have referred to speeches I have made over the past several years on the subject of inflation. Let me make it abundantly clear here and now that I take back not one word that I have been saying in any of those periods on the subject of inflation. Two years ago we were faced, in the view of many people in

this country, with a serious threat of inflation. Indeed, I have had a good deal to say on this subject. But the climate has changed now and what I am saying now, and what leading Liberals have said in their better and clearer moments, is that the major problem now is not inflation; that the threat of inflation has eased and we can address ourselves now more directly to the problem of unemployment.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what Mr. Walter Gordon said recently; he said that very plainly; and that is what hon. members opposite have said in their clearer moments. Hon. members opposite in this debate, however, have been telling us we were wrong to fear the threat of inflation a couple of years ago. They were telling us then that there should have been expansionist policies; they would have introduced expansionist policies then. If they had had the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, the results would have been very serious and damaging. But conditions are different now. Now is the time, however, when hon. members opposite are standing up and criticizing a budget that, in response to the conditions of 1961, aims at expansion of the economy. Now they are critical of an expansionist budget and they have said the most extraordinary things. They have held out the picture of the government turning on the printing presses. Every hon. member opposite knows in his heart that there is no thought on the part of this government of extending any countenance whatever to inflation or turning on the printing presses. An hon. member of this house resorting to the worst kind of buffoonery stood up here not long ago and tore pieces off a dollar bill. I suspect, Mr. Speaker, that as soon as he got out of the house that evening-

-he patched up the dollar bill with scotch tape and probably rushed off to the bank, perhaps even to the Bank of Canada, to present it as a damaged dollar to get back a brand new dollar bill in its place. But after he had finished his performance here he sat down and pounded his desk in applause of his own speech.
They picture this budget as threatening inflation. Well, here is Mr. Walter Gordon who wrote for the Toronto Daily Star on October 15, 1960. He said: "It is unemployment and not inflation that is the immediate menace." How can members opposite contradict Mr. Walter Gordon? Here again the Daily Star sets forth Mr. Walter Gordon's proposals, 12 of them, with illustrations. No. 4 says: "Produce more goods and import less." Hon. members opposite have very short
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming memories. In fairness to Mr. Walter Gordon who has been doing his best to help them they should not repudiate him now in the way they have been doing in this debate. This is a scandalous way to use a very important ally.
They are pretending that the cost of living is going to rise as a result of this budget and they seize on an observation made by a man in the baking business suggesting that the result is going to be an increase in the cost of bread. They have been trumpeting this all over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
