Mr. Speaker, following upon the budget and the decline in the exchange value of the Canadian dollar, the wheat board raised the price of wheat by five cents per bushel. The action taken by the wheat board in increasing its asking price for all grades of wheat and in all positions followed traditional policy and, what is perhaps more important, is justified under existing circumstances. If Canadian wheat prices had not been brought in line with the new exchange value of the Canadian dollar, we would have, in effect, offered wheat on the world market at a lower price and this would have had several results, all of which appear undesirable.
First are the international aspects. Wheat is an international commodity and prices are highly competitive. Any major reduction in the overseas price of Canadian wheat would undoubtedly have been met by our competitors.
Second, there are domestic aspects. It follows that as far as wheat exports are concerned, an increase in the price of wheat was the only feasible alternative if our western farmer is to benefit from the downward adjustment of our dollar. And, Mr. Speaker, the benefit to the western wheat farmer was one of the purposes of this budget. Make no mistake about that.
Let us see this matter in its true proportions. Of course, this meant that Canadian millers would also have to pay a higher price for wheat. However, the impact of this on the cost of making a loaf of bread is very
7222	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Hon. D. M. Fleming small, and it is difficult to see any justification for the claims of at least some elements of our baking industry to the effect that they would have to increase the price of bread to the consumer by one cent per loaf. I understand that an increase in the price of wheat by five cents per bushel will account only for about one eighth or one ninth of a cent per loaf of bread, and a 24-ounce loaf at that. Consequently, the change in the price of wheat, taken by itself, should not lead to a rise in the price of bread. Unless there are other and additional factors which make it difficult to hold the price line, the bakery industry should be able to absorb this increase of one eighth or one ninth of a cent for a 24-ounce loaf of bread. So I do not think we need to be much impressed by these bogeys which are being raised by hon. members opposite.
I have said in the budget speech, and I repeat it now, that in my opinion the effect on the cost of living in Canada as a result of the reduction in the exchange value of the Canadian dollar will be minimal. I repeat that.
I shall not have time to go into detail on the subject of the alternative proposals put forward by the governor of the Bank of Canada but I think I have said on other occasions enough about this to indicate why they were in their principal aspects unacceptable. Let me make one further observation on this subject. When the governor of the bank, in the shocking statement which he put out the day before yesterday and which has been distributed since all over Canada in envelopes of the Bank of Canada bearing the mark of the postage meter of the Bank of Canada, each worth 17 cents postage-when he says in that statement that the budget had been changed as a result of his putting out that statement on Monday he is uttering a monstrous and total untruth.

The budget has been changed many times up to the last minute and there were many changes in this budget, but not one of them had anything to do with anything that the governor was putting forward or with the statement the governor put out on the Monday in violation of the confidence in which that statement was sent to me in February. So this statement on his part is completely untruthful and misleading.
Finally-and I am compressing my remarks-we have before us and are now about to vote upon an amendment which invites the house to express its lack of confidence in the government. It winds up by saying the govern-


ment is not entitled to the confidence of the elected representatives of the people. Nothing could be plainer than that description of an invitation to the house to express want of confidence in the government. It was interesting, however, to find that one new hon. member of the house went a step further. The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss La-Marsh) went a step further. She was not content to ask the house to say that it has no confidence in the government but she said, as reported at page 6923: I can only say, Mr. Speaker: "Take us to the country."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: She meant to the cleaners.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
She continued:
"How hon. gentlemen opposite would then find out what the feeling of the country is... with respect to the trifling proposals which were placed before us on Tuesday night."
And then, when she was asked the question by another hon. member of this house whether she was speaking for her party when she made that remark, she replied:
I am a member of my party. I know they are people of courage, that they have been responsible for a great government, and will be again shortly.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hon. members opposite did not take in quite as much territory in their amendment. This amendment invites the house to say it has no confidence in the government. It could just as easily, if hon. members had wished to do so, have asked the house to say that the country had no confidence in the government. That would have been the fulfilment of the kind of statement which the hon. member for Niagara Falls was purporting to make and she seemed to suggest that she was speaking for her party. Other hon. members opposite have been a little more cautious in this respect but in view of the fact that there has been an example here again of hon. members opposite trying to have it both ways, talking out of both sides of their mouths at the same time, perhaps the house should understand that this is a challenge that goes all the way and we are prepared to meet it on any basis.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Aye.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The question is on the main motion.
On motion of Mr. Mcllraith the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire what the business will be for tomorrow and the rest of the week?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: A continuation of the debate on the budget tomorrow, and perhaps the house will be agreeable to concluding it on that day. Depending on the progress made tomorrow, I will announce the business for Friday and Saturday.
Tell us now and then we will know what progress is being made.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
